subtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS

speechtext: The house resumed, from Monday, July 4, consideration of the motion of Mr. Diefen-baker for second reading of Bill No. C-79, to provide for the recognition and protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Winch.

subtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house rose last evening I was commenting that it seemed to me the bill of rights was divided into two separate sections. In the first place, clause 2 of the bill contains a declaration of the fundamental rights of Canadians as individuals; clause 3 of the bill sets forth the sanctions or the operative part of the bill.
As to the declaration of the rights of Canadians as individuals, it has been said that all the rights that are listed here already exist in the law of Canada. That is true. Indeed, the clause itself says that these rights have always existed in Canadian law. I submit that is the reason the clause "declares" and does not "enact" these freedoms. I think it would have been folly, when these rights and freedoms are already recognized in our law and have been for many years, to have attempted in this statute to enact them.
As to clause 3 of the bill, that establishes a watchdog over parliament and the judiciary to guarantee that these freedoms are not overrun by statutes of this parliament. From now on any man who wants to find out what his rights are need not be a constitutional lawyer or a political scientist able to turn up the cases and the precedents which have been built up over the years. Instead he can turn to the bill of rights. At the same time, if any judge or parliamentarian wants to test any act which has come or comes before this house to see whether it abridges our fundamental freedoms and basic rights, he' has only to turn to clause 3 of this bill.
Clause 3 provides that no enactment by statute in the past or in the future shall be applied or construed so as to submit anyone to arbitrary arrest or imprisonment or to authorize or impose inhuman punishment. It provides the right to counsel. All these things may have hitherto existed somewhere in our law, but now they are spread out in this bill for everyone to see.
As far as we as members of parliament are concerned, I think the most important part of the bill is clause 3. From now on we will watch more closely every bill which comes before us, and every act which has been passed will come under the special scrutiny of the public of Canada and the bench who will see that it does not override the fundamental rights and freedoms of Canadians as individuals. It will also ensure that everyone has fair treatment in any contest between the state and himself.
Now, Mr. Speaker, for a few minutes I would like to deal with the prime objection to this bill which has been raised on a constitutional argument. As I understand it, there

are two ways in which the British North America Act could be amended. First, if this bill were to apply not only in this parliament but in every province of Canada, then the provinces would have to join with the dominion in requesting an amendment to the British North America Act. Then the bill as a part of the British North America Act would apply everywhere throughout the nation and in both federal and provincial fields. Or, the British North America Act could be amended under the 1949 amendment, I think it is section 91 (l)(a), since this bill deals only with matters coming within federal authority, by an address of both houses of this parliament to the British parliament.
With regard to an amendment jointly entered into by the dominion and all the provinces, it does not seem to me that we have any right to ask that of the members of other legislatures. We may show leadership to the provinces, and if they wish to do so there is nothing to prevent them from adopting this bill or similar bills in their provincial legislatures. I do not think it is up to us to interfere in their legislatures or to suggest to the provinces what procedures or practices they should follow. We will have shown them here what we think should be the law of Canada, and by doing so we suggest to them that a similar act might commend itself to them.
Mr. Speaker, I think we would be presumptuous if we asked the provincial legislatures to seek an amendment to the British North America Act which would limit the powers and authority of their legislatures when they are now so jealous, and properly so, of the powers of their governments. After all, why should such a bill be placed beyond the reach of the legislatures of Canada? Why should not members of parliament who have brought forward this bill be empowered to repeal it as regards federal matters? This bill has been sponsored by the public of Canada, and I believe the public of Canada wants to retain the right to amend it, to change it, or to repeal it if they see fit to do so.
As to the second method of amending the British North America Act, this parliament could by a joint address ask the British parliament to amend the British North America Act without the consent of the provinces, inasmuch as this statute refers only to matters within federal concern. But what would be the gain from that? We have spoken so many times during this debate of the constitution of Canada. The British North America Act does not constitute the constitution of Canada; it is only that part of the constitution which
Human Rights
delineates the authority of the provinces vis-a-vis the federal authority, limiting the authority of each.
The British North America Act does not contain the whole constitution of Canada. Most of the important parts of our constitution are not written at all; they come to us from the customs and traditions of many years. Much of the most important part of our Canadian constitution is to be found in a hundred statutes spread through the statute books and in many decisions of the courts which define the rights of citizens and of legislative bodies both federal and provincial.
Mr. Speaker, by proposing that we pass Bill No. C-79 we do amend the constitution of Canada. We set forth in writing rights which heretofore did not exist in the same form in any statute. We establish a special statute of interpretation and make it part of our constitution, so that from now on all federal statutes are tested in accordance with this one.
An amendment under section 91 (l)(a) of the British North America Act gives us no more, as far as entrenchment is concerned, than this bill does today. A section 91 (l)(a) enactment can be amended by a joint address on a resolution introduced in this house and passed also in the Senate, with one debate in each chamber. But to repeal this act would require not only a resolution but in addition first, second and third readings in this house, providing for several elaborate debates on the bill. I firmly believe that the only way any federal statute can be entrenched is by the insistence of the public of Canada that it remain the law of Canada. If at any time the Canadian people want to change this bill they are free to do so, and we would not want to have it any other way. But certainly to amend the British North America Act would give this bill no sacrosanct quality which it would not have after passage in this house.
In conclusion I would like to express my compliments to the Prime Minister, inasmuch as the introduction of this bill and this debate are in a way the culmination of a major portion of his life's work. Over many years and during many sessions he has advocated a bill of rights which would set forth for all Canadians everywhere what their rights are. He has always advocated that bills passed by parliament should be subject to special scrutiny to see that the fundamental freedoms of Canadian citizens were not trampled upon. He has always felt that there should be a statute which at least declared what our basic rights as citizens are so that any man who felt aggrieved could go before a court and point to a statute on the books which

Human Rights
guaranteed him certain fundamental freedoms, like his freedom of religion, his freedom of speech, his right of freedom from discrimination because of his race, his national origin or his colour, and his right to retain what is his until he is deprived of it by due process of law.
This is the principle of the bill of rights. It is an overriding statute to which any individual can flee for sanctuary regardless of orders in council, administrative regulations or so-called emergency situations that arise in the hysteria of the moment. It is simply a specific, basic recognition of the principle that society exists for the individual and not the individual for society. And if any man ever wishes to show that he has been wronged, he will in the future be able to rely on a concrete statute which places his rights as a human being and as a citizen in this land beyond question or doubt.

subtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure you will agree with me that in this debate we have listened to a considerable number of constructive and able speeches. Certainly the hon. gentleman who has just resumed his seat has made a speech that deserves the recognition which I give it as being the careful analysis of a serious-minded member who is dedicated, as we all are in this house, to the principles and the concepts of human freedom.
Whether we agree with this bill in the way suggested by its proposer, or whether we seek to improve it along the lines of the suggestions which have been made, notably by the Leader of the Opposition, there can be no doubt that in all parts of this house every hon. member in every political party is firm in the belief that our society, predicated as it is on the existence and continuation of human freedoms, does present to totalitarian countries a unity of understanding and conviction as to the primacy of the individual in relation to the state.
But we cannot agree with the Prime Minister that the measure before the house will, for the first time in Canadian history, recognize in law the freedom of the press. His actual words were:
-this is the first time in Canadian history that freedom of the press is going to be recognized under law.
That is not an accurate statement of the situation. That certainly is not a correct characterization of the effect of this bill; for the fact is that every human right and fundamental freedom with which this particular measure is concerned is now protected by law in this country. There are now in existence effective legal remedies to protect these human rights in Canada. That has been the
[Mr. MacLellan.l
situation, and that will continue to be the situation after this bill becomes law.
What are the facts? We have in this country inherited the British traditions of government and constitutional law. We have thereby inherited the historical safeguards of the subject. What are they? They are, in addition to Magna Carta, the petition of rights, the habeas corpus act, the bill of rights and the act of settlement. Our statute law, more particularly the growing body of judicial decisions, gives security to the individual as no other measure, I believe, can hope to do. This bill will not change that. This bill will not add something to our legal safeguards which does not at present exist. This bill has the value of being a declaration of the convictions of this parliament with regard to human rights and fundamental freedoms, but I submit that in its present form it is no more than that.
I do not deny the value of a declaration by this parliament of something that has long been recognized in our fundamental law and which, particularly in the last decade, has been recognized in this country by our courts and particularly by the Supreme Court of Canada. I am sure the Prime Minister wants this measure to be, in its final form, the most responsible and effective measure possible. In order to achieve that objective, I do hope that an opportunity will be presented in a committee of this house to afford to those who by training and interest are experts in this field an occasion to offer submissions.
Reference has been made by many hon. members in the course of this debate to the work of those who in March, 1959 put in writing in the Canadian Bar Review their views with regard to the bill of rights now before the house. An opportunity should be given to these gentlemen-to Mr. Lederman, to Mr. McWhinney, to Mr. Bowker, to Mr. Louis-Philippe Pigeon, to Professor Bora Laskin, to Professor F. R. Scott, to Mr. Albert
S.	Abel, to Mr. Donaldson, to Mr. Carter, to Mr. Mundell and others-of appearing before this committee and putting forward their views on this measure. We should have an opportunity of examining the deputy minister of justice. We should afford the opportunity to all the organizations which have made representations to the Prime Minister and the government in this matter to appear before the committee. In other words, nothing short of the most careful examination of this bill ought to be afforded, no matter how long that takes; because in years to come we will have confusion and chaos in judicial interpretation, in judicial lawmaking, if this bill does not emerge in a form

as perfect as it is possible for human beings to contrive by the use of words.
I know the deep interest on the part of the Prime Minister in this bill of rights. He and I have been members of this house for a long time, and I do not deny for a moment that his interest in this subject has been one which reflects his own legal training and his own concept of the role of government in society and the importance of freedom in society without which human personality cannot continue to grow and become truly enriched.
But having said that I say to the Prime Minister that this bill is not the best bill that could be brought forward. The hon. gentleman himself, I am sure, would recognize that if he would recall the words which he uttered at the Canadian Bar Association meeting referred to last evening by the hon. member for Edmonton West, when he said that this bill would be introduced at the beginning of this session and that a joint committee of both houses would be set up to give study to its implications and effect.
This bill is deficient not only for those reasons but because of another weakness. I express a prejudice in this area as a common law lawyer. The bill is deficient in terms of its weakness in reflecting the danger of rigid codification. In saying that I pay my respects at once to the civil law lawyers. There is the danger of restriction in trying to put into the document certain existing rights which will be expanded in the light of new situations, as we now know. The rights we talk about today *-certainly economic rights and legal rights too-are not those mainly discussed in the last century. In a quarter of a century from now, in the light of this nuclear age, who is going to deny that there may emerge new situations that will create at least concepts of new rights and new obligations?
This bill deals only with our political liberties and with some of our legal rights. It does not deal with economic liberties. It deals with freedom of the press, freedom of speech, freedom of assembly, freedom of association, freedom of conscience and freedom of religion. Yes, it deals with all of these things. These freedoms are now guaranteed under the law of this country as a result of the incorporation into our fundamental law of the great charters to which I referred a moment ago, and more particularly the decisions of our courts, notably the Supreme Court of Canada in such instances as the Switzman case, the Saumur case, the Roncarelli case, among others. These cases now have gone far to establish these political freedoms so inherent in our parliamentary system that they cannot
Human Rights
be looked upon as the property of the provinces. One judge has given the obiter dictum that it may even be that this parliament itself could not interfere with these freedoms, although the court has not really pronounced on that subject.
Yes, political freedoms are referred to in this bill, but it is not as a result giving to the citizen a greater security of enjoyment than what is now provided for in the law. Our legal liberties are partly mentioned but not our economic liberties, except for section 2 (a) referring to property. There is no mention nor is there any declaration of the conviction that must stand behind even these newly conceived rights. It may be that it is difficult to put into a charter like this what we mean by economic rights; but at a time when society is evolving and when the political philosophy of every party in this house subscribes to the view of full employment, is it unfair or extravagant to suggest in this twentieth century that we have the right to place alongside our political freedoms, with no less effect, those rights that affect the economic well being of the citizen?
We must not forget that the declaration of human rights to which the Prime Minister attaches so much importance deals in large measure with economic and social matters. The declaration of human rights says that all men have the right to the economic and social discoveries of our age, to the economic and social benefits of our time. The declaration of Philadelphia subscribed to by this country along with all the other United Nations in 1943, declared in as solemn a form as the declaration of independence that the nations that could use their powers and resources to wage war could also use the same powers and resources to provide for economic and social welfare.
I say that a bill of rights is not complete that does not take into account these economic rights. What are they? They are, it is true, tied up in some way with the concept of property, but they go far beyond that. They include such things as the freedom of an employer to hire at rates and under conditions which he may determine. They also include the right of a worker to his job-a proprietary right in his job-and the freedom to strike and to picket within the law, and to bargain collectively. Those are the new recognitions of rights and freedoms which in this day and age cannot be given a secondary place. That was possible in the nineteenth century, but that is not possible today.
Because this bill of rights does not deal with such rights as I see them, it is on that account deficient. Nor does this bill deal with liberty in what one might call its human

Human Rights
rights or egalitarian sense; such things as fair employment practice laws, fair accommodation laws, equal pay for women laws, all laws which emancipate women, the right to election, the right to medical care, the right to disability pensions, and so on. Are we to say that these are not rights? Are we to say that in the objectives we have placed for ourselves we are not to regard these as legitimate aspirations?
They are not absolutes any more than the declaration of political rights and freedoms in this bill can be regarded as absolute. These must be qualified. Freedom of the press is not referred to in the law as an absolute, although in this bill it is referred to as such. Surely in the consideration of the freedom of the press we must take into account that the law has taken in certain qualified safeguards, including the right to take an action for defamation of character, which would be and is a limitation under our law guaranteeing the freedom of the press. And so, Mr. Speaker, the bill is deficient for these reasons. In my judgment an opportunity undoubtedly ought to be given so that we can consider these matters when we get to the committee.
Is it unfair to suggest to the Prime Minister that the bill is somewhat vague and ambiguous in its present form? Are we satisfied, for instance, that the method to which we have resorted in order to incorporate these freedoms is the most effective one? To paraphrase the language of the Prime Minister, we are going to pass a bill that comes within section 91 of the British North America Act. We are not, the right hon. gentleman said, in any way going to interfere with the jurisdiction of the provinces. To that end we are simply passing an act of this parliament, an act with all the ordinary attributes of a bill that might be presented by a government or a private member.
But surely the Prime Minister and all those interested in civil liberties are concerned about the totality of freedom in our country, and not a measure of civil liberties which might be practised in a Canadian railway station, in a uranium plant, or in those areas that come under the exclusive jurisdiction of the dominion. We want to see these freedoms extended and guaranteed all over our country, any place, in any section of our country, and by anyone and for anyone. That is not what this bill does.
We have suggested, first of all through the Leader of the Opposition, that the proper way to bring forward a bill of rights is by embedding it in our constitution. That presupposes an arrangement with the provinces; that presupposes a conference with the provinces and agreement either as to a constitutional amendment through action on the part

of this parliament, or through action by this parliament and by all the legislatures.
The Prime Minister has given no indication that he has endeavoured to try and bring about such an arrangement. It may be that as a result of the study which this committee will give-which I hope it will be able to give-to the bill it will be possible for us even yet to suggest to the government that we ought to deal with this matter comprehensively and with all the legislative jurisdictions which have some responsibility in the preservation of human rights in this country.
There are bills of rights now in Alberta and Saskatchewan. If embodying this idea in the constitution is not acceptable, could we not agree to have a conference with the provinces to discuss these matters; could we not at least make an effort to avoid the divisibility of enjoyment of these rights, so at least there could be parallel declarations by all the provinces affirming their conviction in the general declaration that we make here in this bill? That at least could be attempted.
This bill because of its vague language, such as that contained in clause 2 dealing with the question of property and of due process of law, will, I am sure, provide occasion for much litigation and legal argument. It is regrettable that the bill is limited by being made applicable only at the federal level; for in my opinion these questions of civil liberties should not be treated separately and differently in the various divisions of our country, and I am sure no one, including the Prime Minister, wants to see that kind of impression created or that situation developed.
The bill, of course, has many omissions. For instance, it is not clear in clause 3 what is meant by the phrase "all the acts of the parliament of Canada enacted before or after the commencement of this part". Clause 2 reads:
It is hereby recognized and declared that in Canada there have always existed and shall continue to exist the following human rights.
Then the rights are enumerated. It is not clear that this bill does not in fact in these very words, and particularly those that follow, interfere with provincial matters. Does "Canada" here mean Canada in a geographical sense? I know what the Prime Minister intends. He said in this house it did not; he said this bill was to apply only to matters that came within the competence of the federal government. But the courts, when they come to interpret this bill in relation to other statutes or by itself, will not look at what the Prime Minister said in this house because, under the judicial rules of interpretation, it is not open to any judge, in

order to ascertain the meaning of a statutory word, to make reference to what was said in the debates of parliament or of a legislature. Therefore what the Prime Minister intended will not be applicable or will not assist the judges in arriving at the decisions they will have to make.
There may be something in the argument made by Louis-Philippe Pigeon in the Canadian Bar Review, at page 66, in which he refers to Canada as meaning in the geographical sense. If that interpretation is correct, his conclusion is that this is a violation of section 92 of the British North America Act, and particularly of the property and civil rights clause. If that is the situation, if the language is capable of that interpretation, can we not see at once that trouble is going to ensue in the interpretation of this measure unless this imprecision is corrected? It is for that reason that Mr. David Mundell, Q.C. suggests, among three recommendations that he makes, that not only should this bill be sent to the supreme court for interpretation, but that the language ought to be tightened so that nothing is done in this legislation to interfere with the constitutional powers of the provinces.
The same argument applies to the use of the word "property" in clause 2(a). That is a very important consideration. The Prime Minister says, of course, that what he has in mind is property within the control of the federal parliament, property that does not come within the ambit of the property and civil rights clause in section 92 of the British North America Act. That is what the Prime Minister says and that is the view of all of us in this house. But that will not necessarily be the view of the Supreme Court of Canada or of any other judicial body called upon to interpret this measure. Property and civil rights is a cornerstone of provincial authority in our country. They are as sovereign in the exercise of their competencies under section 92 of the British North America Act as we are in the exercise of our powers under section 91. The trouble that will ensue, that is to say the legal controversy that will develop, let alone the political difficulties that will follow, are so apparent that I would hope that when we do reach the committee stage there will be no difficulty in reconciling the situation.
In my judgment this bill does not modify all pre-existing legislation; at least there is doubt about that. The Prime Minister may have positive views. I am sure that when a court comes to consider a particular grievance and is confronted by a statute such as the Immigration Act and this particular legislation it will decide that because of the general
Human Rights
character of this legislation it must take into consideration and recognize the primacy of an individual statute. Are we to say that as a result of this legislation, for instance, the Lord's Day Act in Canada is going to be repealed? That must be the conclusion if we are to take the view that this bill as it is drawn at the present time will have an overriding effect on all existing inconsistent legislation, or on all future legislation inconsistent with this legislation.

The Minister of Justice undoubtedly has read these learned articles. The minister must know that all these points I have mentioned have been discussed, and that concern exists. I am simply raising them now in the hope that the government, either at this stage of our proceedings or in the committee, will deal with these matters effectively.
For instance, let us take section 2. Are we satisfied that we have a clear understanding of what is meant by "due process"? We are all clear as to what "due process" means but, as Mr. Bora Laskin says, it is not sufficient that a man be assured of protection of his person and property under the protection of due process. It is important that we have a clear understanding of what we mean by "due process". Does it mean due process according to law and, if according to law, according to what law; or does it simply mean in this declaratory statement that it is due process according to certain basic standards of justice? That is very important, because if it is the latter then the citizen is not going
IMr. Martin (Essex East).]
to receive the kind of protection which, under statutes and under judicial interpretation, normally attends the meaning of the words "due process".
What do we mean, for instance, in section
2	when we talk of freedom? True, under the law as it now exists, and as it is going to be confirmed and further declared in this bill, we will have freedom of the press, freedom of speech, freedom of assembly and association; but are these intended as absolutes in this bill, or are we to take into account, or is a judge to take into account the qualifications that now exist as part of the law? When we talk in this bill, for instance, about trials in public, what does that do to the juvenile delinquents act, where a judge may, under certain circumstances, have a hearing in camera? Is that provision to be done away with? These are questions to which we will certainly have to have some answers.
What is meant, for instance, in section
3	(c) by "other constitutional safeguards"? What are they? Where do these other constitutional safeguards now exist in the law? The fact is that they do not exist in the law. Those are words that have a satisfactory implication when first uttered, but they have no legal substance whatsoever.
I could go on and make other observations with respect to what I regard as weaknesses in the bill. The bill does not in any way provide any method by which its provisions can be implemented. A bill of rights will not do away with conflicts between different persons and groups, nor will it remove the need for compromise with respect to many questions in the operation of our law.
There are many things that this bill could do. The Prime Minister was here last night when the hon. member for Edmonton West spoke. The hon. member spoke of the dangerous implications of administrative decisions, and he paid particular attention to the situation in the United Kingdom. He reminded us of the work of Sir Carleton Allen and particularly of Lord Hewart through his book, "The New Despotism". Does this situation not exist in this country? No one has pointed that out more eloquently or effectively in the past than the Prime Minister.

subtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext:
I always gave the Prime Minister careful attention, and whenever he made a submission that I thought was constructive it was generally acted on. But the Prime Minister did not always make constructive suggestions, and

he will be the first to recognize that this is so. If the Prime Minister wishes to egg me on I can go much further in this regard, because I followed with great interest the work of the Prime Minister in connection with the committee that discussed the declaration of human rights and his own particular proposal in 1947 and 1948, under the chairmanship of Mr. Ilsley and Senator Gouin. I know the Prime Minister will have in mind what I am thinking about in that regard, but for the moment perhaps it had better go unnoticed.
The Prime Minister, having spoken of these administrative decisions and their denial of various legal and political freedoms, had an opportunity in this bill to do something about the matter. Why is there no provision in the bill somewhat analogous to the provision adopted two years ago in the United Kingdom and referred to recently by the lord chancellor when he spoke to the bar association of the state of Illinois, and referred to yesterday by the hon. member for Fort William? There could be in Canada as part of this bill a provision such as the United Kingdom now has under the tribunals and inquiries act, whereby a permanent, independent council supervises all government agencies, with special attention being paid to threatened violations. Is that now going to be satisfied by the powers given to the Minister of Justice under section 4 of the bill? The Prime Minister indicates that is so, but surely he is not serious when he nods his head in assent.
Under the bill of last year the Minister of Justice was going to ensure, but under the present bill all he is going to do is ascertain. There is no sanction. All that the Minister of Justice will be required to do will be to examine and see whether any measures have been dealt with that are inconsistent with the general, declared provisions of the proposed bill of rights. There will be no powers given to parliament to cause him to take any steps. In other words there is no sanction and there are no teeth to deal with a situation respecting which certain assignments are given to the Minister of Justice.
In the United Kingdom they go much further. In addition to a public petitions committee, they have recognized the need to supervise administrative or governmental adjudication by means of a tribunal which goes into these matters carefully and is under obligation to take concrete steps. There is need to supervise government regulation and every subordinate lawmaker by means of parliamentary scrutiny or committee. But the
Human Rights
suggested powers given to the Minister of Justice will not in any way deal with the situation.
I therefore say this to the Prime Minister by way of summary. I recognize that as a lawyer he has been interested in this problem for a long time. As he will recall, he raised the matter of a bill of rights when I had the responsibility of introducing the citizenship act. At that time I took the view, from which I now do not stray, that under our common law system, based as it is upon the principle of precedent to precedent, we have a safeguard for our rights that is as effective as anything that is provided for in this bill. Our political freedoms are now provided for in the existing law as interpreted by our courts.
The value of this bill, the Prime Minister and others have said, is in its declaratory character. If we want to give a lesson to new citizens, as was suggested, or if we want to bring home to our young and to the citizens of this country at large the value of our heritage of freedom, we could surely have done it in a declaratory way but in a way that would be more memorable than that which is provided for in the dull words of a statute of this house. We could have sought at least to imitate the language of the great prose writers of the nineteenth century, such as Bentham and Mill, who dedicated their lives and writings to the principle of human liberty. Mr. Speaker, at the time of the luncheon adjournment I was attempting to explain why it is preferable not to attempt to include in this or in any other bill of

Human Rights
rights all the different rights and freedoms to which the citizens of Canada are entitled. It would be particularly difficult to set out in legislation the economic rights of Canadians. This would cause confusion because these rights, whatever they might be, are preserved under clause 5 of the bill, which makes quite certain that no existing human right or fundamental freedom is abrogated or abridged. The Canadian public should understand that it was not the intention to enumerate in this bill all the rights and freedoms. It should be clear that it was not intended to undertake to define them in detail, whatever they might be. Clause 5 reads:
Nothing in part I shall be construed to abrogate or abridge any human right or fundamental freedom not enumerated therein that may have existed in Canada at the commencement of this act.
As I understood the Leader of the Opposition, his chief criticism of the Prime Minister's bill of rights was that there should be greater strictures on use of the War Measures Act. We are not introducing the War Measures Act today nor seeking to have it amended. The Liberal government lived under the act for years and did not choose to amend it. If the Leader of the Opposition feels that this act should be amended, there is a time and place to do so; but it has no connection with the bill of rights. The reason the bill of rights refers to the War Measures Act in clause 6 is so that in the event of war, parliament will first have the opportunity of discussing that proclamation declaring war. That is as far as it goes. If my hon. friend the Leader of the Opposition is as confined in his strictures, as he seemed to have been, to criticizing the War Measures Act and the various clauses in connection with it, I think it is a compliment to the author of the bill of rights that the hon. gentleman had to go so far afield in an effort to find something to criticize.
The bill to amend the Defence Production Act was fought vehemently in the parliament of 1955 and finally passed on the insistance of Mr. Howe, the then minister of defence production. Sections 23 and 24 of that act in particular are for the house an example of the arbitrary measures which will be found to be ultra vires once this bill of rights is passed. The Defence Production Act was amended in 1955, just two years before the previous arbitrary government was thrust from office. The two sections to which I made reference were not renewed. Section 23 made it possible for the minister of defence production to require a person to participate in a defence contract whether or not he wished to do so. Under section 24, where it was deemed necessary for the purposes of the act, the minister by notice in writing could take
tMr. Walker.]
possession of or requisition any supplies whether or not the owner of those supplies wished to surrender them. I respectfully suggest that due to the present government such arbitrary measures are no longer the law. This is an instance where the bill of rights when enacted will automatically take hold and become effective.
At this time I should give proper recognition to the C.C.F. group. They have always been in favour of a bill of rights. It is not very often that I have the opportunity or the desire, to compliment them. Although the manner in which they would envisage enactment of a bill of rights is impossible of fulfillment, nevertheless their general ambition and desire in this connection is proper and commendable.
What are the effects of the bill as summarized? In the first place, it focuses the attention of the public on civil liberties. In this rapidly changing era, when mobs of students have taken over what appeared to be sound and stable governments in the past few months, it is about time we had some idea in the mind of the public concerning what are our civil liberties. We should know, too, what rights the bill seeks to define. The educational effect of this bill on the public will be tremendous. Where in Canada can there be found in an act a list of the fundamental human rights and freedoms accessible to the ordinary layman? Where else can he look to examine these things and say "These are my rights"?
The fundamental freedoms and human rights cannot be changed either secretly or inadvertently as a result of this bill. In my earlier remarks I discussed in detail the reasons for this. This act when in force will superimpose on every act, past, present and future, and on all regulations under every act passed by the dominion parliament all four freedoms and all human rights. This bill of rights acts as an interpretative rule for the courts in Canada to follow in dominion legislation. I discussed that in detail in my earlier remarks.
Finally, this bill enshrines in a statute for the first time in the history of Canada the rights of the individual. July 1, 1960 was really a momentous day of perhaps greater importance to Canada than we can appreciate at this time. Once passed, every Canadian can pick up the bill of rights and say, "Here are my rights and here are my freedoms." When was there ever before an opportunity for Canadian citizens to do that? What a tremendous thing it is for the youth of our country, for the new Canadians who

did not know what fundamental freedoms meant in the countries from which they came?

It is our own earnest hope that as time unfolds, with an appreciation of what a bill of rights can mean when it is fully understood by all the people of Canada, we shall have something which covers not only the dominion but all the provinces. In the meantime, I respectfully submit that this is as far as we can go at the moment, and it is a very long way to go in the circumstances. It has taken 18 years to bring this bill to fruition. In this connection we have one person and one person alone to thank for educating the Canadian public so that they demanded it, and for educating the Liberal party so that they, too, are in favour of it. That this bill be not now read a second time, but be it resolved that this house is of the opinion that the provinces should be consulted in order to ascertain whether agreement can be reached on the terms of a constitutional amendment to guarantee human rights and fundamental freedoms.
I have listened with a great deal of interest to the contributions made on July 1, yesterday and this morning to this debate. In my opinion the issue now before us is over and above partisanship, and I regret that the Minister of Public Works was the first speaker in the debate to introduce partisanship. Before the lunch hour I heard nothing but a bunch of rubbish, utter unadulterated nonsense and political partisanship in its lowest degree.

subtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext:
Referring and pointing to the bill, the Minister of Public Works intimated- and these were his words-"There is our guarantee". Yesterday, the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi said, when referring to the bill, "It is enforceable". I have great reservations on whether there is actually any guarantee in the bill before us, or whether it is enforceable at all. The Minister of Public Works also said about the bill, "Here are my rights; here are my freedoms". I doubt the claim of the minister in this respect, and I also doubt his statement that we have one person alone to thank for the bill. I doubt that the Prime Minister is so vain that he would claim that he alone is the only one we should thank for the emergence in parliament at long last of a bill of rights. I believe he will admit that many other Canadians are equally responsible for the debate that is now taking place, even though he was instrumental in introducing the bill at this time.

I believe that much of the optimism expressed yesterday, this morning and on July 1 may be based on rather weak grounds. In looking over the bill I am disappointed in a number of respects, and I believe my disappointment is shared by a good number of the Canadian people. Before dealing with these disappointments I should like to pay a tribute to the men and the few women who have been responsible for adjudicating upon Canadian law over the years. I believe that our courts have gone a long way and have done much to enhance the liberties of each and every one of us. I should like to pay a compliment to these people, because in the precedents established in Canada and in the United Kingdom over the course of the centuries I believe many more rights are embodied than will ever be conferred upon individuals by this legislation.
I know there is always a dividing line between what constitutes freedom and what constitutes licence, and that it is very hard to determine. I do not think any member of the house would say that we should endorse licence. However, I believe we are all sincere in our desire to enhance the cause of individual liberties and freedoms.
The bill now before us has been delayed for a number of years. It is an important bill, and I do not regret for one moment the delay that has ensued. Rather than introducing a bill of this kind and of this significance in the dying weeks of the session, I believe it might have been advisable to delay it a little longer. I believe that the bill should go before a committee, and I welcome that course of action. However, I express regret that, simply because of the pressure of time, the committee is going to be limited in hearing adequate representations from Canadian organizations and individuals who are interested and would like to make a contribution to the deliberations of the committee.
I express disappointment in the bill of rights now before us because I feel that the mountain has laboured and has produced a mouse. I believe that the bill is uninspiring, and I heartily endorse the views expressed by the Leader of the Opposition yesterday in this regard. If the bill is meant to express our ideals, I believe it fails utterly in that respect. If it is to be taken as an expression of our ideals with regard to individual freedom, then all I can say is that I believe we can do much better. I believe there are thousands of Canadians with the ability to express our ideals more adequately than they are expressed in the wording of the bill. If the bill is to be a law, it is inadequate in that regard. It is neither an expression of an ideal nor will it be an adequate act or law of the House of Commons. It falls far short.

It seems to me a placenta, an afterbirth; and, as I said before, the mountain has laboured and at long last has produced a mouse.
It is my contention that Bill No. C-79, an act for the recognition and protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms, is unworthy of the vision that the Canadian people had of the member for Prince Albert in 1957 or 1958. I submit that the bill is unworthy of our heritage. I submit that it is unworthy of the significance of our Dominion day, July 1.
This bill is supposed to protect the fundamental rights of the individual, but I notice that in clause 2 it says that-
-there have always existed and shall continue to exist the following human rights and fundamental freedoms, namely,
(a) the right of the individual to life, liberty, security of the person and enjoyment of property, and the right not to be deprived thereof except by due process of law.
I should like to emphasize the words "except by due process of law". These words make a mockery of any pretence that the individual is now being protected against actions on the part of governments. Anything that is done by a government ought to be by due process of law; and while the bill may protect my rights from invasion by another individual, it does nothing to protect my rights from invasion by government because the government always has at its disposal the due process of law. In my opinion the whole reason for the origin of the bill falls down right here in this clause, which contains the words "except by due process of law". I am being allowed to enjoy my fundamental rights with this exception, "except by due process of law". I have those rights only as long as the government of the day deems it advisable that I have them. I feel that the whole intent of the bill is defeated by that little inclusion "except by due process of law".
We have in this bill no protection whatsoever against the law. The law can violate individual human rights at any time a parliament or a government deems it advisable to do so. In the whole bill-and this is repeated and underlined time after time in the bill- the prerogative of the government and of parliament to violate individual human rights is maintained. Any argument that this bill is going to protect individuals from arrogance or from arbitrary decisions on the part of government falls apart like a house of cards.

subtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext: How so?

subtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext:
Because, as I indicated previously, the rights are guaranteed "except by due process of law". In other words, the right to own property, the right of life itself, the right of liberty or the right of security of the person can be nullified by due process of law. I do not think that basic contention can be denied.
However, I was going to advance beyond that point. We are even limited in the protection of our rights in so far as individuals can continue to deny us these rights without hindrance. The most I can say is that if my rights are being threatened by another individual, I can appeal to the courts and I may toe able to get an injunction or a restraining order. I will say that much on behalf of the bill. However, beyond that I cannot go. Individuals may violate this bill and there is no penalty attached to the violation. They may be found guilty of violating the bill. However, next week they may repeat their offence and they may repeat it the week thereafter. There is no enforcement. There is no recourse except the possibility of withholding an intended action by appealing to the courts and asking for an injunction. The only teeth in the bill, as I see it, are the possibilities of appealing to the courts when one anticipates that the bill may be violated. There is nothing else in it that will enforce the bill.
I therefore find it extremely hard to understand what the Minister of Public Works means when he says that this is our guarantee, and what the hon. member for Brome-Mis-sisquoi means when he says that it is enforceable. I do not realize how it is enforceable when individuals can continue to violate the act ad nauseam, and when the government can use the due process of law in order to

Human Rights
deny to individuals the fundamental rights that are established in the bill.
I especially support the amendment because of the reply of the Prime Minister on July 1 to the question asked by the hon. member for Assiniboia. In reply to the hon. member for Assiniboia the Prime Minister made it abundantly clear that the provinces had not been consulted. I feel that this answer indicates that the bill now before us is less than the best that we might offer to the Canadian electorate at the present time. Apparently no effort was made to obtain the agreement of the provincial governments. Not only do I believe that an effort should have been made in this direction, but I also believe that a bill of rights, in order to be really effective, should be submitted by way of a referendum to the Canadian people at the next general election, especially if there might be hesitancy on the part of one or more of the provinces in reaching agreement on what constitutes or should constitute a bill of rights for the Canadian people as Canadian citizens.
I do not place too much reliance on provincial bills of rights. I do not believe that a Canadian living in one area of Canada ought to have rights that he is not able to enjoy in all other areas of our nation. It is obvious that the government did not even bother to consult with the provinces. They were so intent on making this a bill of their own that they have produced a bill that I consider to be partly a proclamation or a declaration. If it is meant to be that, any master of the English language would say it is a horrible failure in that it does not express our ideals. If it is meant as a law, it is unenforceable and is extremely weak indeed.
The bill in effect does not affect existing legislation. I realize that there is a direction to the courts. However, I believe that any member of the Supreme Court of Canada would say that the direction contained in section 3 of part I of the bill is as wide open as a barn door. There is really no specific order to anyone connected with our judiciary to be found in section 3. It does not affect existing legislation effectively. There is no direction to a court. It does not affect future legislation because under clause 4, as has already been ably pointed out, the minister "shall examine". It does not order the minister to do anything; he shall merely examine, which means nothing. There is no directive there except that he shall examine. It does not say that he shall declare something ultra vires; he shall do nothing except examine. There is not even the order that he shall report to this House of Commons, but merely the order that he shall examine. He

can examine until he is blue in the face; if the government has made up its mind it wants to do something it may listen to his advice or it may not, depending on its whim at any particular time.
At this time I would like to ask our Prime Minister where is the committee that he spoke of on January 27 last? At that time our Prime Minister said, as reported on page 390 of Hansard:
I felt and I still feel that one matter that might well be brought before the house would be the setting up of a committee similar to that in the British House of Commons known as the scrutiny committee. It would examine legislation being passed by parliament and already on the statute books, and would examine orders in council, which are not passed by parliament directly, to the end that anything in the nature of a contravention of fundamental freedoms would be brought to the attention of the house as a whole.
At this time, almost six months later, we have heard nothing more of this committee which was supposed to be established. Where is this committee? I asked a little later, on February 4, whether this proposed committee would also examine or be responsible for examining the regulations of the department of immigration. As recorded on page 715 of Hansard I said:
Is the Prime Minister in a position to inform us when we may expect the establishment of a scrutiny committee, such as he announced on January 27; and will this committee be permitted to investigate alleged discrimination because of colour in Canadian immigration regulations?
The answer I received at that time is as follows:
Mr. Speaker, the first question is the only one I can answer at this time.
Actually the Prime Minister answered both questions.
When we arrive at that point in the proceedings and I am able to bring about agreement with the members of the opposition as to the establishment of this committee, then, if it is agreeable to the house, the committee will be set up.
I would like to interject here a question to the Prime Minister. Has he consulted with the opposition, or how many more months must the opposition wait for him to consult with them as to the establishment of this committee he offered to set up? The Prime Minister continued:
As to what it will look into and its powers, I think what the hon. gentleman has in mind has not been the usual practice followed by the United Kingdom scrutiny committee.
In other words, as I read that it is obvious that the regulations of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration are to remain exempt not only from the provisions of the bill of rights which is now before us but also from the eyes of the proposed scrutiny committee about which the Prime Minister waxed so enthusiastic only six months ago.

As I see the bill before us, if it is really going to have some teeth it will mean that Canadians of East Indian origin are going to have the same rights as all other Canadians in the matter of bringing in their relatives. Canadians of Chinese or Japanese origin are going to have the same rights as, say, Canadians of Norwegian or Dutch origin when it comes to bringing in their relatives. If the bill has any teeth at all it will mean a radical and automatic revision of existing immigration regulations.
I believe it will also affect our efforts in regard to world refugee year. I am dismayed and angered every time I watch the television appeal on behalf of world refugee year when refugees in the Middle East are shown on the screen in pictures depicting their deplorable state, and similar pictures are shown of the likewise deplorable state of refugees in Hong Kong. While the dollars are lured out of our good-hearted Canadian taxpayers on behalf of world refugee year, the money is devoted exclusively to the admission into Canada of white refugees living in western Europe.
If the bill of rights means anything at all it ought not only to put an end to this misuse of advertising and the wringing of the hearts of Canadians on behalf of Middle East and Hong Kong refugees, but proper use should be made of the money obtained instead of using it only on behalf of the white people of the world. This government stands guilty of utter discrimination in this regard, and the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation stands guilty of utter misrepresentation of the whole cause of world refugee year and its appeal for funds.
Much has been said on behalf of Canadian citizens of Japanese origin. I would like to say this, and I do not think it has ever been said before since this government has been in office. You cannot grant equal rights to Canadians of Japanese origin until you right a wrong that has never been righted yet. I refer to the confiscation and looting of the assets of Japanese Canadians. I know very well that under the Liberal government an inquiry was held into this matter and many of these wrongs were righted. However, when the offending party could not be located there was no equity restored to the Canadian citizens of Japanese origin who had suffered an undue wrong.
I refer now to the looting of the warehouses in the custody of Her Majesty in Vancouver, when pianos and living room sets were simply stolen; when forest rights were sold for a song to avaricious Canadians; when farms worth tens of thousands of dollars were sold for mere hundreds of dollars, and equity has not yet been restored. Canadians of Japanese origin will never feel 79951-0-362
Human Rights
that they have been given a square deal until the day, and I hope I live to see it, when the conscience of the Canadian people will move the government of the day to restore to our fellow Canadians that which was so wrongly taken away from them.
I would like to see in a bill of rights a certain measure of protection to the Canadian people from brainwashing. At the present time, because of wealthy advertising interests and monopoly in the field of communication, the Canadian people are being brainwashed indeed. I believe that in a bill of rights there ought to be a decree which would protect our young from being brainwashed. I know people do these things in all innocence, but high school teachers will hand out propaganda to their pupils, and even Sunday school organizations accept the film put out by the B.C. Electric Company in British Columbia, though interwoven throughout the film are the glories of this so-called wonderful organization. Canadians today, especially the younger Canadians, are helpless in the face of the brainwashing that is taking place.
I see no reason why a bill of rights should not also contain economic rights as suggested by other speakers, including the hon. member for Assiniboia and the hon. member for Essex East. I believe there should also be a guarantee in the bill of rights to every Canadian who is willing to work and to every Canadian who, though willing to work, is unable to work through no fault of his own, providing for a basic minimum standard of living; and that should include income, pension, education and health insurance.
It was many years ago that the leaders of the western world in the now famous Atlantic charter announced that one of the ideals of the democratic world was the establishment of freedom from want. I see no reference in this bill of rights to that announcement which was made in time of war. Many years have now gone by, and I contend that what was expressed as an ideal in wartime ought also to remain an ideal in time of peace. Our people must be free in order to progress.
I should like to close by submitting that all progress throughout the ages has always originated with a minority. It has never been in the interests of those in authority to advance mankind; it has never suited the vested interests to do so. It has always been the aim of vested interests to obtain for themselves control of government in order to block progress and maintain the status quo. Above all, it has never been in their interest to remove ignorance and fear.
I feel that the bill now before us is a move in the right direction. I feel, too, that

Human Rights
the amendment is well worth support. However, I regret that after all this effort something more worthy of the expectations of the Canadian people has not been presented at this time.

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre Sevigny (Associate Minister of National Defence):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I take
great pleasure in rising in this house to express a few personal views on the bill of rights now being discussed.
I believe it is quite desirable to deal with this matter and to reaffirm our faith in the principles which are at the basis of our very life.
I also believe that it is essential for us, the representatives of the people, whatever our political allegiance, to come here and reaffirm loudly in this national parliament what we repeated and even promised many times to those who wanted to listen-to come here, in this house, and state in a loud voice that we are here to serve the most significant rights of the citizen, to serve freedom and to serve democracy.
A very great American, Thomas Jefferson, once said that a bill of rights such as the one we are now discussing is not necessarily effective in all circumstances but that it would always be useful, and almost always effective.
I, for one, think it is necessary for all of us to unite and to reassert in this house our determination to serve the best interests of democracy and freedom.
It is often said, Mr. Speaker, that a great many crimes have been committed in the name of freedom, and unfortunately, one has to admit it, that struggle for freedom and that fight for human rights have caused many crimes.
But this is due to the fact that this freedom, so dear to all of us, and for which we must fight, is worthy of the greatest efforts, the mightiest struggles and the hardest fights. It is our duty to protect it at all times. The safeguard of that freedom, this is our life's ideal, our prime purpose.
Let us remember those far-away days of 1918 when, after four years of bloodshed, the war that was supposed to end all wars was coming to a close.
Then, the victors and vanquished alike declared that, after so many efforts, sacrifices and bloodshed, the free world should realize that human rights and freedom were finally being protected; and with an utter unconcern,

countries plunged into a frenzy of pleasures and enjoyment, without giving a second thought to the impending disaster.
Barely 21 years later, the civilized world again found itself in the midst of a war that is considered today as the greatest conflict of all times.
Again in 1945, after all those sacrifices, we all thought: now it is all over, at last human rights are protected. There is no further need to talk about them. War is a thing of the past; there will never be another.
Yet what do we see today, Mr. Speaker? Again we see the known world hovering on the very brink of a conflict which, if it happens, may well involve the destruction of all mankind as we know it. In view of that very grave danger still hanging above our heads, I feel there is a need to reaffirm our faith in the life principles in which we believe. I feel there is a need to proclaim out loud to the face of the whole world that we, here in Canada, believe in freedom and justice.
We are often inclined to say that all the wrongs are on the enemy's side. And it is a fact that, behind the iron curtain, millions of men are living in latent slavery; that millions of men dream only of the day when perhaps a ray of light will brighten their lives and bring them those spiritual freedoms which they know we enjoy. It must be recognized, however, that our side does not hold a monopoly on virtue. All too often we see cases of monstrous intolerance which could quite easily lead so-called democratic countries, which we regard as brothers, into the abyss of communism. Therefore it is to avoid what is happening in those friendly and allied countries that we, in Canada, must affirm and reaffirm our belief in those principles which are the very basis of justice and peace.

Mr. Speaker, there is no doubt in my mind that the standard of living of the communist countries has been considerably improved during latter years. It is quite possible that some day the eastern nations will know a standard of material comfort almost comparable to what we are accustomed to, and which unfortunately we accept with such insouciance and carelessness. It is obvious that the leaders of communist Russia and China are striving and working to acquire material wealth for the citizens of their country.
That is why it frequently happens that so many economists and so many people who, heaven knows, should know better, seem to find some good in the doctrines under which these countries live. Sometimes we see some industrialists, professional men or others who

come forth and declare that the system under which these countries live is perhaps not so bad, and they suggest that maybe we should study it more closely. There are those among us who at times may be influenced by this propaganda, and there are some who dream of the day when this system of life will predominate in the world.
There is no doubt that the arguments of these propagandists may have a certain influence on the minds of our population. Today, I do not hesitate to say that what is too often forgotten is that this race toward material wealth and comfort is never accompanied by a similar race toward the attainment of spiritual values. It should be realized that the enslavement of the minds of men and the complete restriction of their right to think, to speak and to pray God as they wish to pray God have always been the aim of the way of life of the communist countries, and these things are in direct opposition to what we believe. If our population could only appreciate the extraordinary value of these rights which we enjoy, and which we too often accept without giving them a second thought, I am sure the communist ideals would never prevail in our land. I am equally sure that these people would realize that the bringing into effect of a bill such as the one before us is an absolute necessity.
In former years I travelled twice behind the iron curtain. Although I admit that during my travels I was received with the greatest courtesy, I nevertheless realized how strained the atmosphere can be in these totalitarian lands. I saw with my own two eyes what fear means. I never saw two people express controversial views in front of each other. Never did anyone confide anything to me unless he was alone, and unless he made sure that no one was within earshot. I know what it means to be scared when you touch a telephone. I know what it means to look for microphones in hotel rooms. I know what it means to be suspicious of the man next to you in the restaurant. I know, because on the few occasions when I could actually speak to someone alone they told me that every move of their every day life must be careful. They must watch themselves because they never know whether a brother or friend is actually an enemy.
At the slightest suspicion the state police grab these people, shut them up with no further explanation and release them if and when they feel that this can be done. I repeat that although I was treated with courtesy, I saw what fear was. I saw fear in the eyes of men, fear in the hearts of women, fear and jealousy of what we have in our land, in this land blessed by God 79951-0-3624

Human Rights
this way, we would make many friends and draw nearer to those people who, if we are unable to help them, are bound to be attracted by the bait held out to them by communist nations.
Moreover, Mr. Speaker, I support this bill of rights for still another reason, one of no lesser importance. Indeed, I personally believe that every truth deserves to be told, retold, reiterated and repeated. To my mind, even on this American continent, it is necessary to state and repeat frequently that we believe in equal opportunity for all and in an ideal of freedom and justice.
Oh yes, Mr. Speaker, many hold the view that the things that happened in the old countries in Europe cannot happen here in Canada. It is stated by many that the developments taking place in other commonwealth countries are restricted to countries abroad and that we cannot possibly fall victim to similar situations.
Yet, Mr. Speaker, nothing is further from the truth. Nothing is further from the truth because we in Canada, as well as people in the United States or elsewhere in the western world, are faced today with the same danger that threatens those other countries. The first of those dangers is intolerance, racial intolerance, intolerance that prompts some people, for reasons of colour, religion, or origin, to mistreat other human beings who, being born in the same country, are entitled to share equally in the privileges existing in those countries.
Does a week ever go by, Mr. Speaker, without our reading in daily newspapers reports of intolerance either in the United States or Canada? Can we say that our entire population is free from those feelings that lead citizens in various sections of our nation to regrettable excesses.
Mr. Speaker, we in the commonwealth regard ourselves as civilized nations; yet just recently, because of racial intolerance, bloody riots have taken place in another commonwealth country caused by the fact that leaders in that country displayed intolerance towards a majority of the people. We now suspect that if this intolerance should continue, a whole continent might very soon be put to fire and sword.
Mr. Speaker, is it not true that hardly 15 years have elapsed since the end of the greatest conflict in history? Is it not true that, at the end of that conflict, we heard of unbelievable acts of savagery committed by a supposedly civilized nation? I am not going to blame the German people for the things that happened in their country from 1939 to 1945; I will not blame them because it might have happened elsewhere. I simply want to say this:	if we often restate

to our people the principles of life that are the basis of our existence, if we say to our children: you are as free as your neighbour, you have no more rights than he has, but you have as many privileges; if we ward off the menace of hunger and of fear; if we advocate and reassert the advantages of living in an atmosphere of freedom of speech and of thought, I venture to think, Mr. Speaker, that we shall exert a good influence and that we shall prevent some ruler, sooner or later, from taking over the government of our country, from encroaching upon our rights and submitting our democracy to a dictatorship such as those we have witnessed and suffered from.
Germany was one of the most civilized countries of Europe. I must say again that I do not blame the German people for the excesses committed from the time Adolf Hitler came to power until his downfall in 1945. But I submit that once a country disregards the value of the principles of life that must guide it in the choice of its rulers, that country runs the danger of falling under the rule of tyrants and dictators who might easily commit the same crimes of which the nazis were unfortunately guilty.
A very short time ago, in the light of the Eichmann incident, we have had to live over again the atrocious history of concentration camps. Nowadays, as in 1945, it seems frightful that such things could have taken place, but it must be admitted, for it is grim reality. And this happened barely 15 years ago, in a civilized country which unfortunately, by a conjunction of circumstances, fell under the rule of a ruthless dictator.
What occurred elsewhere 15 years ago, is happening today in a commonwealth country. The incidents we read about every day in the papers can easily happen here. It is therefore essential that we have a bill of rights as a solid basis for the principles of justice, freedom and equality in which we believe.
There are some people in this house, Mr. Speaker, and also elsewhere, who say that this bill is unnecessary, that it only duplicates the Bill of Rights of 1689, that it is a copy of the Magna Carta, of the American Declaration of Independence and a mere repetition of old rigmaroles and old stories of which we are surfeited. However, Mr. Chairman, nothing could be further from the truth, because I think if something is really true, it deserves to be told and retold.

Yes, Mr. Speaker, if mankind had more often remembered the great principles that were taught 2,000 years ago from a small mountain in Judaea, perhaps we might have avoided those mass slaughters, those wars to which we unfortunately were eyewitnesses and in which we even fought.
Mr. Speaker, you know as I do that 2,000 years ago, the greatest of all men preached from that mountain the simplest yet most beautiful of truths which, through millions of repetitions, have retained all of their original truth, beauty and purity.
Every day, those simple truths proclaimed by Jesus are repeated, such simple truths as "Love one another", "peace on earth to men of good will", "do not do unto others what you would not have them do unto you". In all their simplicity and beauty, those truths have retained their freshness, and for that reason they deserve to be repeated, just as we should repeat our faith in our way of life, in our freedom, in our right to worship God in our own way, to speak the language we learned at our mother's knee. We should repeat them and repeat them often; otherwise, we will unavoidably be drawn into chaos, disorder and neglect as were those nations who forgot those great truths.
It is often said that such truths are not so very important, not so very serious. Why waste time in platitudes and high-sounding speeches when everyone knows perfectly what it is all about. May I, before closing my remarks, give you an example of the power of words and the power of determination not to surrender to any threat however powerful and tyrannical. We remember, Mr. Speaker, that in 1940, one man, alone, perhaps the greatest of the twentieth century, Sir Winston Churchill, rose, uttered simple but powerful words, and repeated to the flagging forces of democracy: "We shall not flag nor fail, we shall fight on the beaches, we shall fight in the streets, we shall fight everywhere the enemy may be. We shall fight on. We shall never surrender, and victory will be ours because the forces of good are with us." Is it not true that those magic words of Sir Winston Churchill succeeded in electrifying a whole world which then set to work; and is it not true that this marked the turning point of a battle which could otherwise have been an absolute defeat?
