Mr. Speaker, on the last occasion when a similar bill was before the house, as well as on this occasion we have heard, and no doubt will hear, very eloquent and forceful addresses on this most basic subject. I had the privilege on the last occasion of making some observations on that bill, and I should now like to supplement what I said then. While the addresses that we hear

are most eloquent and, as I said, forceful and laudatory, it strikes me as if some of our colleagues seem to think there is a contest as to whether or not the bill deserves support. I should like to submit that there is no contest here as to whether a measure of this kind is a desirable one. I do not think there is anyone in the house who will contradict that statement. However, I am afraid that we have taken our eye off the target.
It is my respectful submission that what we should be concerned with is an examination of this legislation in order to see whether it contains those ingredients or those clauses which a bill of this kind should contain. I should like to suggest that we should address ourselves principally to the question of whether the measure is in the form in which it can attain all of the objectives sought by every member in this house. Of course the bill repeats all the platitudinous hopes, dreams and aspirations since Magna Carta in the year 1215; later the English bill of rights in the year 1689, the French declaration of the rights of man proclaimed in the year 1789; even more recently the preamble to the United States constitution and to some extent the Gettysburg address; and similar pronouncements by nearly all countries in the world.
There is but one basic difference, Mr. Speaker, namely that the others were all unanimously accepted and approved by all the people and all the sections of the countries in which they were proclaimed and became the particular constitutional bases of those countries. The present bill lacks exactly that unanimity and constitutional strength which the others have had, and that is the matter which concerns us. It may be a pretty and pious hope to present a piece of legislation of this kind. However, let us see whether it is effective or whether it can be effective.
I would point out that only the unanimity which accompanied the other legislation in the other countries can give this measure any meaning and effectiveness. Otherwise it is just a repetition, as I said, of pious hopes which have been stated and repeated in this house many times. The bill itself is not fundamental. It is not a part of our constitution, nor is it even suggested that it can become a part of our constitution. To me the measure itself lacks permanence. It can be repealed at any time. It is only an act of parliament. It is quite obvious that it does not retain that permanence that a constitution has.
Moreover, to me the measure also has another shortcoming. As has been said in so many different ways, it lacks soul and it lacks heart. To mean anything it must be a piece of legislation that will be ingrained into the very fabric of Canadian conviction. It should

be taught in all schools and should be almost religiously accepted by all Canadians. I do not think it can achieve this permanence by this rather prosaic, unrealistic, unimaginative and unappealing language.
It must be accepted by the parliament of every province without a single exception. Otherwise how can we protect people against invasion of civil liberties by provincial legislatures which enact laws in connection with matters over which they have constitutional jurisdiction such as property and civil rights. In this chamber this very morning we heard of a very poignant and classic example of how it is possible to have a conflict between federal legislation and provincial legislation which basically defeats a bill on human rights. We heard today that three people, with skin of a different colour from ours, were denied admission into a hotel in Canada. The Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) eloquently and justly took the position that a thing like that should not be permitted in this country. When my leader asked him whether this is in conflict with his bill of rights the Prime Minister did not answer whether there was or was not any conflict with his bill of rights. All he said was that it was a matter that falls under the jurisdiction of the provincial legislatures.
You have here a classic example indicating that the bill now before the house would not and cannot remedy the situation about which we heard this morning, quite coincidentally. If the federal parliament had the authority to enact legislation which could remedy a situation of that kind I am sure the Prime Minister would have had such a provision in his bill. He did not say so in so many words, but I noted that he was visibly disturbed by the incident. It was an unusual incident to happen in a country that is presenting a bill on human rights and fundamental freedoms. Surely the Prime Minister was disturbed by it. Yet he tells us almost, in language out of his own mouth, that this bill of his that he is presenting to the house cannot remedy such an injustice as this which we should not have in Canada.
As I said, we support the measure in its theory and its principles but we say that, unfortunately, it does not remedy those faults which exist in Canada and which the bill should remedy. It may be able to go that far; it may be able to reach into those avenues in which these unfortunate incidents happen if it were studied and presented in a form which will make it constitutional so that it will become a basic part of our constitution.
It has been suggested by a number of hon. members who have spoken that this might be done, either by a conference with the
Human Rights
provinces or by other means. I would point out that there are many examples of such conflicts. It should be the duty of this house -and we are all concerned-to find a correct constitutional measure and we should give study to the matter.
In addition to the other suggestions that have been made as to how it could become constitutional, I would not hesitate to suggest that the government should appoint a royal commission on which would be represented provincial legislatures and constitutional law authorities, and that they should sit together, consult with each other in order to work out a proposal for a bill of human rights and fundamental freedoms. When it is approved by this royal commission, let each one of the members go back to their own legislatures and present that bill which has been unanimously accepted and found to be constitutional. If each legislature without any exception will approve that measure, then we have unanimity in the country or a form of unanimity which can then make it constitutional. Then we have it incorporated into our constitution and there we have something of permanence. What we all seek is a constitutional and political guarantee for a complete and comprehensive bill of rights and not a political, personal or academic exercise in political science.
The measure should supersede narrow and parochial legislation or regulations on immigration, refugees, stateless persons and the like. Legal scholars and constitutional lawyers and recognized authorities have given their carefully studied opinions that the present bill falls far short of being constitutional or one that can be effective in any way.
That is a serious thing for members of the house to consider. I do not think it is a waste of time in going through this exercise. I think there have been some splendid speeches and the more we talk of these things the healthier it is for the country, but let us not close our eyes and say that just because this has been presented it is the best thing. It is not the best thing. Constitutional lawyers have pointed out that legally it will not stand up.
I should like to address myself for a few moments to the point that the bill falls far short of being completely comprehensive. May I point out a typical illustration of what I have in mind. I am not going into the clauses in detail but I will have to refer to them to illustrate. In clause 2 we find this language:
It is hereby recognized and declared that in Canada there have always existed and shall continue to exist the following human rights-

Human Rights
I draw the attention of the house to those words. They are there as if to say that no other rights than those listed in this clause have ever existed in Canada before, that these are the only rights which have existed in Canada. I do not admit that. We do not know what the rights are in precise language. If, for example, instead of saying "the following human rights" you said-
Could I draw the hon. member's attention to clause 5 of part II?

I will come to clause 5 of part II, but this is the language we are dealing with. If this clause had read that there has always existed and shall continue to exist in Canada all the known human rights, including the following, that language would be all inclusive. We would have been sure that that would cover every conceivable human right, whether listed in clause 2 or not. The Prime Minister, being an able lawyer, will readily see that there is a difference. He is stating to the world that these rights which are mentioned in clause 2 have existed in Canada only up to the present time.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Read clause 5.

I have read clause 5 and I will come to it, if the hon. member will be patient for a few moments. I cannot ignore clause 2.
Then a little further down in clause 2 we find:
(b)	the right of the Individual to protection of the law without discrimination by reason of race,-
Et cetera. To me that is faulty because it appears as if the individual has the right to the protection of the law against discrimination by reason of race, colour, and so on. I submit respectfully that the bill of rights should clearly declare that the individual has the right to be free from discrimination by reason of race, national origin, colour, religion or sex. He should have the right to be free from all these things and to the protection of the law when his rights are invaded. But to say that he has the right to the protection of the law could imply many things which are not intended. If you were to say that the individual shall be free from discrimination by reason of race, colour or creed and that he shall also have the right to the protection of the law when these rights are invaded, that to me would be a very complete statement.
Then lower down we find:
(c)	freedom of religion;
That is all it says. I would prefer to see the words "freedom of religion to profess and practise it according to one's own belief and conviction". A man may have the right to

freedom of religion but may be prevented from professing it or practising it, and I think that is another fault. I suggest that when we limit our rights we have to examine them minutely and carefully to make sure nothing is overlooked.
Then we have in (d) freedom of speech. I would prefer to see the words "freedom of speech, but not to incite treason or hatred amongst men". We have heard it said that people who make violent attacks in speeches against others have freedom of speech, a right to their own opinion. But we have no reason to incite hatred amongst men and we can say so by reducing that to writing and putting it in a bill of rights.
Then we have in (e) freedom of assembly and association, and I say that that is faulty also. It would have been complete if it had read "freedom of peaceable assembly and association". I think that would make it constitutional and much more acceptable.
Then we have (f), freedom of the press. Again I would include here "but not to incite or unlawfully malign". Under the heading of freedom of the press many scurrilous pamphlets and magazine articles are written and circulated in Canada. I am sure that every time members of the house see them on their desks they must be stirred and wonder why it is that such horrible literature is permitted to go through our mails. Attempts have been made to stop the circulation of these pamphlets. Literature is a very good thing but the moment it starts to incite race hatred and hatred amongst men, when we circumscribe these rights into a bill of rights the people who are guilty of those activities should be clearly told "You have the freedom of the press but you have not got freedom to malign people, to circulate scandalous and scurrilous literature to preach hate amongst people and between one Canadian and another." That is not freedom of the press. I am the last in this country who would in any way obstruct freedom of the press or freedom of speech, but when these things are reduced to the point where they are taken advantage of and do more harm than good, then while writing a bill of rights we should write it with all the clarity and security we possibly can.
I also say that I believe there have been many freedoms which have been omitted from the bill. There have been some observations made by some hon. members, but not one of them have included the phrase "freedom of work" and "freedom of trade union association". That is sometimes questioned. Either a man is free to do that or he is not. If he is not, let us not be afraid to say so. We should say that an individual should have freedom of work or freedom not to work,

because if I have not freedom not to work and I am forced to work, that is slavery. Surely that is not intended. Therefore this measure should contain the provision that there shall be freedom to work or not to work.
Next, I would suggest the addition of a further provision to this clause entitling students to seek enlightenment at institutions of learning regardless of race, colour or creed. That should be clearly stated in the bill. There was an instance, which has already been mentioned in this chamber, where a man of oriental origin applied to three universities, which he named, for permission to study medicine, but he was refused admission to each of them. If a man wishes to study he should have the right to study and should not be refused admission to places of learning because of his race or colour. I do not think we want ever to reach a stage where there will be segregation in any of our educational institutions, and that should be clearly stated in our bill of rights-that there should never be segregation of students in our schools.
There are a number of other matters that need careful attention, although this may not be the time at which to carry out such a process. There are so many flaws which are apparent in this measure that some mention must be made of them and a really dangerous situation arises when a list of specific rights is drawn up and put down in such a measure as this, in which it is said: these are your rights in addition to any others which have existed. I refer hon. members to clause 3, subclause (e) where a person may not be deprived:
-of the right to a fair hearing in accordance with the principles of fundamental justice for the determination of his rights and obligations.
A fair hearing by whom? The wording should continue "by an impartial tribunal, and/or a court of law". If that is what is wanted, then spell it out.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I shall be glad to explain that when we come to the committee stage. It was not intended to give the minister of justice dictatorial power, but merely to ensure by an expression of parliament that the minister of justice, whoever he might be, does carry out his duty with regard to the review of legislation and regulations.

I do not think anyone has ever questioned whether or not the minister is performing his duty in examining the legislation that comes before the house. Here it states clearly that:
The Minister of Justice shall, in accordance with such regulations as may be prescribed by the governor in council, examine every proposed regulation submitted in draft form to the clerk of the privy council pursuant to the Regulations Act and every bill introduced in the House of Commons, in order to ascertain whether any of the provisions thereof are inconsistent with the purposes and provisions of this part.
My question is this: supposing the minister comes to the conclusion that a regulation or a bill is inconsistent with those provisions-what will the minister do? Or suppose the minister comes to the conclusion that it is not inconsistent, what will the minister do? This clause is really meaningless. I can believe that the minister would examine it and give it a fine, academic, legal examination. To make the provision meaningful it should provide that after examination by the minister, if he concludes it is inconsistent he should say so and make a report and reject it. I see no purpose for this clause being included.
There should exist in Canada a parliamentary committee like the one that exists in other countries. I was discussing this matter today with a member of one of the Australian legislatures who said that they have a committee which supervises and investigates possible abuses of purely administrative powers and the regulations which are established by order in council. We have no such committee in this parliament.
An act of parliament gives a minister the right to set up regulations for the administration of his department or for the discharge of that particular measure. The regulations are set up, passed by order in council and move into the law of the land without being scrutinized or discussed by parliament. It is these regulations that should be examined by a committee of this house. It would be helpful if we had a committee like those which

exist in Denmark, Australia and in the mother of parliaments to examine and scrutinize the regulations which become part of the law by order in council whether we like it or not. I do not know whether the regulations should be examined before being submitted to the governor in council for approval or after they have been passed but they should be scrutinized at some stage. It is necessary to assess them because some of them may be abusive. I could cite instances of regulations which almost have the effect of nullifying existing legislation or rights.
Perhaps I should give one illustration. I refer to the law adopted last year concerning humane slaughter. I shall only repeat what I said then. I am speaking just as an individual. I have freedom of religion and the bill before us will affirm this; yet, through the regulations of a department there might occur an invasion of my right to enjoy freedom of religion. That is the kind of regulation that should be examined by a committee of this house composed of members of all parties. The committee could reach a conclusion as to whether or not, whether intentionally or inadvertently, there might come into being an abuse of a human right or an interference with a fundamental freedom which it is intended that Canadians have.
One hon. member who participated in the debate said that the present bill is without any sanctions. This bill when passed will be a law. It does not represent a preamble to the constitution. It is not even a constitutional provision. This is a bill of parliament which it is intended that people should obey. With respect to other bills passed by this parliament there are sanctions if people break the law. What are the sanctions in this measure? Again it is reduced to a pious hope.
I do not object to the bill. I should like to see it enacted as I am sure all hon. members would. However, I do feel that it should be more enforceable, that it should have more teeth in it. It would win my more hearty approval if we could, so to speak, really spread the gospel by making it a bill that all Canadians could fully understand.
One hon. gentleman said that this may be an important beginning. Certainly the Magna Carta and other measures of that nature were the beginning of an important trend and have achieved great significance over the years. I think the Prime Minister would do the country a great service and would make a significant contribution to humanity for all time to come if the hon. gentleman would accept my suggestion of establishing either a royal commission or a

special commission composed of the finest brains on the subject we have available in the country as well as representatives of all the provinces to see if they could hammer out a bill of rights and fundamental human freedoms that would be acceptable to all. As long as a measure of this nature is not acceptable to someone it is not a true bill of rights.

Mr. Speaker, it is perhaps fitting that I should participate in this debate because in the last few months I have had a special preoccupation, not with the theory of human rights and fundamental freedoms but with the actuality and practice of them. In that time I have seen a woman driven to insanity. I have seen babies born illegitimately. I have had a person come before me and cry her heart out for two hours because she could not resume her proper name and thus secure a passport to go behind the iron curtain to her homeland. These things I have seen and these things were affected by fundamental freedoms and human rights.
If I could have had in that harrowing time the privilege of coming here to the House of Commons and knowing that I was among friends and that everybody shared the zeal that I do that people's rights should properly be protected, then I would have been happy and proud to have been a member of the House of Commons. Instead, those things have been denied me, not by the theoretical words of anybody but by the practices they have carried out. I intend to say more about that later as I discuss the Canadian bill of rights which is before us for consideration this afternoon.
First may I turn to the criticisms made of this bill by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson). I will quote his criticisms and then, if I may, reply to them. The hon. gentleman is reported at page 5651 of Hansard of Friday, July 1, 1960, as saying:
Historically, Mr. Speaker, I think there is a good deal to say for Professor Lower's contention that there has never been any serious abridgement or any attempt to abridge what are generally understood to be human rights and fundamental freedoms by the parliament of Canada in time of peace or non-emergency.
Perhaps that is quite correct but the Leader of the Opposition on that occasion spoke immediately following the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) who in his remarks set forth nine examples where human rights had been abridged by the actions of the government in recent times. If you say they were not abridged by parliament that is probably so because parliament in those days did not stand up and censure the government when it derogated from 79951-0-3634
Human Rights
human rights; but if you say that all those occurred in wartime, as the Leader of the Opposition would suggest, then that is wrong because six of the nine examples cited by the Prime Minister occurred in the years immediately following world war II. A wartime spirit of autocracy may have been there to promote these things but those were days of peace when those derogations occurred.
Another member of the opposition, the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) spoke this morning about economic freedoms, the right of employers, as I gathered his words, to hire as they saw fit on conditions they saw fit and to pay wages they saw fit. If this is an economic right, it is just a reflection of the laissez-faire Liberal doctrine of the nineteenth century which has long ago been rejected in our society when we ensure that the working man does have rights against too powerful employers.
Then, the final Liberal speaker who just preceded me, the hon. member for Cartier (Mr. Crestohl), spoke about the language in the bill of rights. Later on I will say more about the language in the bill of rights and about some of the suggestions made to cure it. He suggested that it should be in more lively language, something that would capture the imagination. He then proceeded to read into the record a series of suggested changes that he himself had thought of which would make this bill of rights, if those changes were adopted, hobble like a centipede with 99 peg legs.
Now, to the C.C.F. The other day the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge), described himself, I gathered, as Snow White, in his desire to have things done properly, and the seven dwarfs around him nodded their agreement; Gabby, Doc, Doleful, Snee-zy, Grumpy, Dopey and Slaphappy all agreed with him, and I take it they all agree with the remarks that have been made by the C.C.F. speakers in the debate so far. Freedom, rights, liberties; do not let them get away with what they are doing to the natives in South Africa; the rights of people in Hong Kong. These sonorous words flowed from their lips, Mr. Speaker, from the lips of a group which cannot manage the affairs that are right in the hands of this parliament.
Let me turn now to the language of the bill of rights and to the critics who suggest that more memorable words can be captured somewhere else. Let me read you this Mr. Speaker, for simple, short expressiveness:
Every person and every class of persons shall enjoy the right to acquire by purchase, to own in fee simple or otherwise, to lease, rent and to occupy any lands, messuages, tenements or hereditaments, corporeal or incorporeal, of every nature

Human Rights
and description, and every estate or interest therein, whether legal or equitable, without discrimination because of the race, creed, religion, colour or ethnic or national origin of such person or class of persons.
I believe that the only standard words they left out of this are easements and water courses. Where did this come from? That stirring call to set men's hearts alight? It came from chapter 345 of the revised statutes of Saskatchewan, 1953, and section 10 thereof.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Is that the Saskatchewan bill of rights?

It is the Saskatchewan bill of rights, as the Minister of Justice asks. I presume they would present this phraseology to us as the answer to the language that should be employed in this bill of rights.
The hon. member for Essex East suggests that perhaps we could spruce up this document with some preamble from the Magna Carta. I actually believe what he had in mind was the preamble to the charter itself. If so, I shall read it into the record and we shall see if the language will be of any assistance:
John, by the Grace of God, King of England, Lord of Ireland, Duke of Normandy and Acquitaine, and Earl of Anjou, to his Archbishops, Bishops, Abbots, Earls, Barons, Justiciaries, Foresters, Sheriffs, Governors, Officers, and to all Bailiffs, and his faithful subjects,-Greeting. Know ye, that We, in the presence of God, and for the salvation of our own soul, and of the souls of all our ancestors, and of our heirs, to the honour of God, and the exaltation of the Holy Church and amendment of our Kingdom, by the counsel of our venerable fathers, Stephen, Archbishop of Canterbury, Primate of all England, and Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, Henry, Archbishop of Dublin, William of London, Peter of Winchester, Joceline of Bath and Glastonbury, Hugh of Lincoln, Walter of Worcester, William of Coventry, and Benedict of Rochester, Bishops; Master Pan-dulph, our Lord the Pope's Subdeacon and familiar, Brother Almeric, Master of the Knights-Templars in England, and of these noble persons, William Mareschal Earl of Pembroke, William Earl of Salisbury, William Earl of Warren, William Earl of Arundel, Alan de Galloway Constable of Scotland, Warin Fitz-Gerald, Hubert de Burgh Seneschal of Poictou, Peter Fitz-Herbert, Hugh de Nevil, Matthew Fitz-Herbert, Thomas Basset, Alan Basset, Philip de Albiniac, Robert de Roppel, John Mare-schall, John Fitz-Hugh, and others our liegemen; have in the first place granted to God, and by this our present Charter, have confirmed, for us and our heirs forever;-
This is the preamble which perhaps the hon. member for Essex East would like to smuggle into the bill of rights. If not, and he wants language from elsewhere, perhaps this from the great charter, section 55, would do the trick nicely:
All fines have been made by us unjustly, or contrary to the laws of the land, and all amerciaments that have been imposed unjustly, or contrary to the laws of the land, shall be wholly remitted, or ordered by the verdict of the 25 Barons, of whom mention is made below, for the security of the peace, or by the verdict of the greater part

of them, together with the aforesaid Stephen, Archbishop of Canterbury, if he can be present, and others whom he may think fit to bring with him; and if he cannot be present, the business shall proceed, notwithstanding, without him; but so that if any one or more of the aforesaid twenty five Barons have a similar plea, let them be removed from that particular trial, and others elected and sworn by the residue of the same twenty five, be substituted in their room, only for that trial.
That might be the replacement that everybody is after for the Income Tax Act. Even this greatest section, section 12, suffers again the defect of language:
No scutage nor aid shall be imposed in our kingdom, unless by the common council of our kingdom; excepting to redeem our person, to make our eldest son a knight, and once to marry our eldest daughter, and not for these, unless a reasonable aid shall be demanded.
And finally, for his edification, so that he can use some of these phrases when he presents amendments to the Canadian bill of rights, I give to the hon. member for Essex East No. 39 of the great charter:
No free man shall be seized, or imprisoned, or dispossessed, or outlawed, or in any way destroyed; nor will we condemn him, nor will we commit him to prison, excepting by the legal judgment of his peers, or by the laws of the land.
The latter part of this section is now known as due process of law.
This time I turn to the Thinkers' Library for inspiration and I recommend this to my hon. friends of the Liberal and C.C.F. parties, the Thinkers' Library, that is. There were suggestions that we follow some of the language of John Stuart Mill. I have his book "On Liberty". There are words in here that are applicable to the present debate but I do not suggest that the language could carry out the purposes of the hon. member for Essex East. For example, I turn to page 16 of this very fine essay and I throw it out not only for the thought it contains, which is ample, but also to ask the house whether it could usefully contain any phraseology for our bill. Mr. Mill puts it this way:
Apart from the peculiar tenets of individual thinkers, there is also in the world at large an increasing inclination to stretch unduly the powers of society over the individual, both by the force of opinion and even by that of legislation; and as the tendency of all the changes taking place in the world is to strengthen society and diminish the power of the individual, this encroachment is not one of the evils which tend spontaneously to disappear, but, on the contrary, to grow more and more formidable.
Obviously within that sentence, and it is a complete sentence, there exists in Mr. Mill's language the problem we are trying to solve, thanks to the Prime Minister's bill of rights. I also suggest to the house that nowhere in that language is there a ready, quick phrase that could usefully be incorporated in the legislation we are considering today.

For those detractors of the Prime Minister and the draftsmanship that has gone into this particular bill of rights, may I also read from another noble work in the English language on liberty, and this concerns liberty of the press. I suggest that the remarks of Mr. John Milton in Areopagitica have particular application to the critics of the Prime Minister. From the Pitt press series, page 34, I am again going to read one sentence which will take about three minutes to read but which contains very powerful language indeed. These are the words:
When a man writes to the world, he summons up all his reason and deliberation to assist him; he searches, meditates, is industrious, and likely consults and confers with his judicious friends; after all which done, he takes himself to be informed in what he writes, as well as any that wrote before him; if in this, the most consummate act of his fidelity and ripeness, no years, no industry, no former proof of his abilities, can bring him to that state of maturity, as not to be still mistrusted and suspected, unless he carry all his considerate diligence, all his midnight watchings. and expense of Palladian oil, to the hasty view of an unleisured licenser, perhaps much his younger, perhaps far his inferior in judgment-
I think these words about unleisured licensers certainly apply to the unleisured critics we have had here.
-perhaps one who never knew the labour of bookwriting; and if he be not repulsed or slighted, must appear in print like a punie with his guardian, and his censor's hand on the back of his title to be his bail and surety, that he is no idiot or seducer, it cannot be but a dishonour and derogation to the author, to the book, to the privilege and dignity of learning.
Mr. Milton's noble words have embraced in one vast sentence a great number of ideas, but again not containing the type of language which people could readily read or understand to be their particular rights.
I come now to one of the problems that I wish the bill of rights could handle and I hope that some time it can be made to deal with this problem. There are areas of responsibility which are given unto men but those areas of responsibility can be carried out properly or can be carried out badly indeed depending on whether men use their frailties or use their strengths to carry them out. Any due process of law should be a dignified process and it should ensure justice. It should be done for the suppliants before it and not for the glorification of those who are charged with the task of performing that judicial function. Theirs not to collect press clippings; theirs to do their duty. A sham judicial process is one where the spirit of the judge is mercurial and wilful and causes or determines not by rules of law but by the toss of a coin or a feeling of prejudice or a feeling of whimsicality, a feeling of caprice.
Human Rights
I have mentioned some of the social mischiefs that derogate from human rights and fundamental freedoms. I hope that by the time 5.30 comes around I will be able to walk out of this chamber, hold my head high again and say that all within this room are fair and just and honourable, not in a platitudinous way but in respect of the practical things that count in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to say a few words in relation to the bill of rights now before the house I find myself in the rather unusual position of following an hon. member who has taken a line somewhat similar to mine. Fortunately I have some other examples of draftsmanship which will reveal as unnecessary the additions which the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) would have us make to the bill.
The hon. member for Essex East has said that the courts have formally enshrined in our Canadian law certain freedoms without the aid of parliament and in so stating he quoted among others the Jehovah's Witness cases. I should like to point out to the hon. member that in the two cases involving Jehovah's Witnesses which came before the Supreme Court of Canada there was a split decision. In each case the judges divided five for the decision and four against, which leaves us wondering how clearly the laws, practices and customs of our fundamental rights are enshrined in human knowledge and in our precedents in Canada. I wonder what might happen in the future if the court is differently composed and if other individuals sitting on the bench have to deal not with exactly the same problem but a similar one. I think the examples which the hon. member for Essex East quoted were of no assistance to his case but merely pointed to the fact that it is necessary to have stated in clear words what the intention of parliament is as to fundamental rights and freedoms.
Another example which the hon. member for Essex East used concerned criminal charges as they are dealt with in the bill, by clause 3, subclause (f), relating to the determination of a criminal charge against an individual. The hon. member asked what would happen in the case of a charge against a juvenile under the Juvenile Delinquents Act. I would point out to him that the Juvenile Delinquents Act is very clear on this matter. The act says that a juvenile delinquent is not a criminal and has not committed a crime. Section 3, subsection 2, of the act reads as follows:
Where a child, is adjudged to have committed a delinquency he shall be dealt with, not as an

Human Rights
offender, but as one in a condition of delinquency and therefore requiring help and guidance and proper supervision.
Therefore I suggest that any thought that a juvenile charged under the Juvenile Delinquents Act would come under this section as a criminal is very far afield.
A third objection was raised by the hon. member for Essex East and by several other members in the opposition. The hon. member for Halifax (Mr. McCleave) in reply quoted certain matters he wanted to bring to the attention of the house. The main complaint is that the language is too simple and too concise, and that it should be enlarged and made more specific in certain aspects.
Just in order to find out what people in the past have thought about the question of drafting legislation, I turned up one of the most valuable books on legislation, namely "Practical Legislation" by Lord Thring, written many years ago. In his introduction he points out that simplicity and clearness of language is the most important point in drafting legislation. At page 2-and this refers to the Magna Carta-he states the following:
The prince of all draftsmen, Stephen Langton, the Papal Legate, expressed Magna Charta in short and precise language; for example, no one can complain of ambiguity or verbosity in the most famous of all written enactments which declares, when translated, "To no man will we sell, to no man will we deny or delay, right or justice."
A little further on Lord Thring points to some examples of enactments in which too much verbosity is included and where things go wrong. At page 3 he quotes an amendment proposed in 1865 which reads as follows:
"Every dog found trespassing on inclosed land unaccompanied by the registered owner of such dog or other person who shall on being asked give his true name and address, may be then and there destroyed by such occupier or by his orders."
Further on in his introduction Lord Thring makes this statement:
The bill should be clear and should state at the very commencement the important principle of the measure and the greatest pains should be taken to separate the material from the comparatively immaterial provisions.
He concludes this page of notes with a warning to all those would-be draftsmen, and I think it is pertinent to the particular case in point:
It may be well to warn the draftsman that in his case virtue will, for the most part, be its own reward, and that after all the pains that have been bestowed on the preparation of a bill, every Lycurgus and Solon sitting on the back benches will denounce it as a crude and undigested measure, a monument of ignorance and stupidity. Moreover, when the bill has become law, it will have to run the gauntlet of the judicial bench, whose ermined dignitaries delight in pointing out the shortcomings of the legislature in approving such an imperfect performance.

I think it might be well to add that Lord Thring seemed to feel that such objections to simple language would come from the back benches. However, today we have had them from the front benches as well.
In connection with the amendment which is before the house, it has been suggested that the consent of the provinces ought to be secured before proceeding with this legislation. The hon. member for Timmins (Mr. Martin), in making this suggestion, compared the present piece of legislation with the amendment to the British North America Act with reference to the retirement ages of judges. He said that if it were possible for the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) to secure consent of all the provinces to that amendment, it should be just as simple a matter to secure consent to the present bill of rights.
I submit that there is no comparison whatever. There are two main differences. The Judges Act amendment is a simple alteration in the constitution on which a decision yes or no can be made by the provinces. The bill of rights, on the other hand, has a number of extremely important principles involved, each one of which must be considered by the provinces and answered yes or no. There is also a more fundamental difference, of course, namely that the amendment to the Judges Act is not what one would call a fundamental matter but an individual instance where consent could be obtained. The bill of rights is basic and as such a basic matter it includes many provisions, any one of which could provide an effective snag to negotiation.
I do not want to repeat what was said by the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker) in connection with previous meetings that had been held in an effort to get the provinces together with the federal government on such basic amendments as the present one. However, I feel-and many other members have expressed this opinion here yesterday and today-that we must have a start on the bill of rights. We must entrench it in our legislation and we must make clear what we intend; then we must hope and expect that in due course the provinces will come along and follow it up.
There is one final approach to this problem that I should like to make and I believe it has not been considered previously. I think we must go on the assumption that this bill is going to pass. I seem to feel that everyone here is in agreement with the basic principles of the bill. Various matters have been raised in connection with minor amendments or changes of wording. Perhaps some of these suggestions have merit. A committee

could consider them, whether it be the committee of the whole house or any other committee. However, those are minor matters. We are now considering the general principle of the bill, and I feel that the bill is bound to pass.
Protestations have been made by the opposition but I feel that no real matters of substance have been raised. It has been said that we should try for a constitutional amendment, that the wording of the bill does not go far enough, that the bill goes too far, that the language is too broad and that it is not sufficiently clear. However, in spite of all these objections, I feel that the bill will pass.
I think we must consider what results will flow from the passage of this bill. I think the results that will flow from this bill are much greater in magnitude than has been indicated by any hon. member of the house in discussing the bill other than the Prime Minister who introduced it. I think it may be many years before the effect of the bill gradually catches up with the legislation which is now on the books and the legislation which may come in the future. I think we must ask ourselves into what valleys and hidden corners of 93 years of Canadian legislation this bill may extend.
Passing reference has been made to sections of the Immigration Act and the regulations. Certain hon. members made reference to other acts which may be affected. I believe there may be many more which have been passed, and forgotten-and are at present unused but which may from time to time in the future make themselves noticed and be tested on this bill of rights in the courts. I wonder what present or past acts of parliament, or future acts, may be washed aside under the influence of the bill of rights.
Those who say that the bill does not go far enough may be surprised to find that it goes very far and that its effect may be reaching forward for a good many years. I feel the bill sets a level of morality in legislation in this country, a level which has not been previously set down in words. We have had from time to time expressions in the courts as to what is right and just and what are our basic human rights. These depend in large measure upon what judges can find in past cases and what they personally feel about these measures, but there has been no guide on which they may found their decisions. I see this bill as giving them that guide and that level of morality in considering whether an act does contravene basic human rights.
Mr. Speaker, if the house will forgive me for being poetic. I see the bill of rights
Human Rights
as a river flowing into a large valley, filling in many nooks and crannies which have been previously unnoticed, washing away many of the legislative bills which have been based on very sandy and shaky foundations in the past. I feel it may be many years before the full extent of this flowing in of the bill of rights into our legislative procedure will be fully determined and understood. Many years will pass, I believe, before this process is complete; but in the end, we will look back on this bill, as we now look back on the other great landmarks of declaratory legislation, as one of those great additions to the earlier declarations of human rights which have always been ours.

speakeroldname: Mr. Egan Chambers (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with some hesitation that I rise to follow so many learned members of the legal profession who have spoken on this bill. On the other hand it is not too often that we have an opportunity in the House of Commons to talk about and vote upon matters as fundamental as is this bill of rights. Many of the matters which come before us call for a judgment, a comparison. We have, for instance, the estimates of a department which come before us and we must try to judge or decide whether the amounts of money required are appropriate. We must judge whether the business could be done with a little less money or whether it would be better done with a little more.
But today we are dealing with something that is not in the realm of judgment but in the realm of basic belief. We have before us a measure that enunciates principles, the principles upon which our society is, or certainly should be, founded. The bill before us sets out in black and white the things that Canadians believe. It sets out those things upon which we have built this country and it will be the guide post as we continue to build in the future.
There have been some criticisms of the language. To me, the language, and particularly the language in part I, is admirable in its economy. It is clear, concise, and beyond misunderstanding.
The world today is divided between those who believe that the only things of importance to mankind are the material things and those who believe that the spirit of man and his dignity as an individual are of first importance. It is time that the people of this country through their parliament should declare before the world to which of these camps they belong. Here we set down in the clearest of terms a statement of Canadian principles for all to see.

Human Rights
One of the other criticisms which has been made is that this bill may be repealed or that future legislation need not necessarily conform to it. But I ask you, Mr. Speaker, which member of this house today should he become a minister would rise in his place and introduce a bill to repeal this bill of rights? Which member of this house on occupying a seat on the treasury benches would rise and introduce a bill containing the clause "Notwithstanding the provisions of the bill of rights"? I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, it will be a long, long time before any Canadian minister will rise with any such suggestion, and that if any minister did so the ensuing debate would indeed be a fundamental one.
We have also heard some niggling criticisms to the effect that such a bill is not required. The legalistic mind insists that these rights are already embodied in British common law which we inherit, that we are safe in the hands of our courts and our tradition of freedom.
Mr. Speaker, how can I tell my sons what it means to be a Canadian in terms of court decisions? How can I explain to men of other countries Canada's position on these matters in terms of the supreme court's decision in the Alberta press act? The objections to this bill come from the same source that objections to progressive steps have ever come. They come from the comfortable, from those who have in their own resources the ability to defend their rights. In their own position in life, economic and otherwise, they are unafraid.
This bill is not for the comfortable, except incidentally. This bill is for the protection of those who need protection. It guarantees to the weak and to the poor their freedoms. With part I of this bill I can explain to my sons what it is to be a Canadian; I can explain to men of other lands why I am proud to be a Canadian because, as I said before, in the simplest and most direct language it is set out in a few brief lines that:
It is hereby recognized and declared that in Canada there have always existed and shall continue to exist the following human rights and fundamental freedoms, namely, the right of the individual to life, liberty, security of the person and enjoyment of property, and the right not to be deprived thereof except by due process of law; the right of the individual to protection of the law without discrimination by reason of race, national origin, colour, religion or sex; freedom of religion; freedom of speech; freedom of assembly and association; and freedom of the press.
Mr. Speaker, no one in this house has suggested that our rights and liberties stop there, but it is true to say that on these foundations all our rights and liberties are built. I will vote for the bill, not because

in its terminology it is better than some other bill, not because through a process of logic I find it acceptable; I will vote for this bill and its principles because I believe in it.

The
very interesting discussion which took place this morning produced an exchange between the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker) and the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) concerning the debating practices of 35 years ago and this brought to my mind a debate held about that time ago between a team from Oxford and Cambridge and a team from the University of Alberta. The resolution debated on that occasion was:
That in the opinion of this house there is a growing tendency on the part of government to invade the rights of individuals.
This growing tendency perhaps has been established in years gone by. This legislation seeks in my opinion to arrest that tendency. It cannot be denied that there is in this country a marked lack of knowledge as to the rights of individuals. I listened yesterday with a great deal of interest to the contribution made by the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort (Mr. Rapp). He spoke of new Canadians. He told us he was a new Canadian, and he asked us, in effect, to establish for him a statement of his rights and that this bill seeks to do.
May I say that I am a new Canadian. I was not born in this country. My father brought me to this country when I was a very small boy. From my recollections of his struggles, and from my observations over the years, I have come to the conclusion that there was discrimination in the early days of Canada against individuals. In my own part of the country we have a large number of farm operatives, labourers, and workers in various trades, who have come to Canada in recent years, and in the minds of many of these people there is a fear of the law, a fear of the police and, to a degree, a fear of the banks of this country.
Some of us can remember, when the war loans were being raised in the second world war, calling on farmer after farmer, trying to interest them in the purchase of war bonds. I had the experience of being successful in my endeavour to sell some of these bonds, and I recall that when I began to write out a cheque for the value of the bonds someone would say to me: No, I will not pay by cheque. Then he would disappear for a few moments, perhaps carrying a lantern with him, and return later with a tin full of bills, and he would pay for those bonds in cash. That was fear. It does seem to me, as one interested in persons of this type and as one who perhaps has the trust of some persons of this type, that it will be a lot easier for me

on my return home to be able to say to them: I can now explain to you very simply and very quickly what are your rights in Canada.
This in my opinion is a magnificent piece of proposed legislation. It clarifies a great number of questionings. It gives us something concise, something easy to explain to those who perhaps have not enjoyed the education which some of the rest of us have enjoyed, and the Prime Minister is to be heartily commended for his contribution.

It gives me a great deal of pleasure to take part in this debate. I will just take a few minutes. The Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) expressed the hope that all members would have time to enter into this debate and I think the subject has been covered very nicely by a number of members who have spoken already. I have enjoyed it very much.
This bill has been well talked over, but there are one or two points I should like to make starting with a statement introduced by the Prime Minister about changing the nation to what it ought to be. That is just what the Prime Minister is attempting to do. Other words we have heard have been from the official opposition complaining about the wording and the preamble of this bill. The flowery words that are wanted by the members of the opposition are hardly in keeping with some of the things they have said during the times they have been on their feet. The leader of the official opposition, in what I understand was one of his first speeches, moved a very flowery amendment which is recorded in Hansard of 1957-58 at page 3520. I am not going to read it all, because it is very flowery, along the lines of what he thought at that time might go over well in the minds of the people of Canada. I will go down to the bottom of this, and read:
And in view of the desirability at this time of having a government pledged to implement Liberal policies;
His Excellency's advisers should, in the opinion of this house, submit their resignation forthwith.
After all, the Conservative government had been in office for seven months. They had been elected by the people of Canada and right away, after those seven short months, the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) was of the opinion that they should step back and allow him to form a government. In other words, he put all the voters of Canada on the stand. He was criticizing the judgment they had made at that time. He could not sit still long enough to let them enjoy themselves.

This is a very interesting case and one to which some consideration should be given. In my memory I believe that this is one of the first cases where both the respondent and the corespondent have testified to the fact that they committed adultery. I think this raises a point in that the inference could be drawn, although the hon. member for Halifax may object, that the divorce was wanted more by the respondent and the corespondent than by the petitioner.
It has been generally conceded in law that a confession voluntarily given will carry considerable weight except in those cases where the confession would tend to create a situation that the parties themselves wish created. In other words, this confession will give to the man what he says he wants and in that regard I would quote again the following question and answer:
Q. Why did the marriage break up at that time?
A. Well, why make my life miserable and my wife's life miserable when we can't get along? The woman I am living with now I love and I would like to marry her.
In this case we have him stating a motive that may have influenced his confession at this time. I suggest that we should give serious consideration to this type of confession because as a result the respondent is granted the relief that he has said he wishes.

We can see how it would be quite easy to accomplish this result by making arrangements to pay for the divorce if there was violent exception by the plaintiff that the divorce should be given to her and the expenses paid and she would act as the injured party in this case. I am not saying that is the situation because I do not know but it has been generally conceded that confessions that have a stated motive should be looked at with some care because of the fact that they tend not to be in the public interest in that they may cause people to perjure themselves in order to get relief that they could not otherwise get.
I am not saying that this is the case in this instance. I think this young man has indicated that he has some responsibility with respect to his relationship to his wife. It was a shotgun marriage, a marriage by arrangement. He married the young girl only to give the child a name. He accomplished that and I presume there may have been some discussion at that time that if he carried his responsibility that far there would be no further problem. Probably the arrangement was carried out equally well by both parties until the young lady reached the time when she again wanted to try her hand in the matrimonial realm, distasteful as it may have been to her in the first place. It is not usual for both the corespondent and respondent to come forward and, taking advantage of the full protection of the law, make such an admission involving testimony that they have committed adultery. If this happens in too many cases I think we will be warranted in taking a very close look at the situation because it could be an indication that divorces were being sought by arrangement and as a result we should not necessarily give too much weight to the evidence of the witnesses and the confession they voluntarily make.
I notice the hon. member for Edmonton West is questioning this statement. His legal mind may not recognize the fact that people would do this. I presume that Mr. Cohen thinks that that falls within the expression "On or about the 22nd of May", but I submit he could have chosen the 22nd, the

20th, the 21st, the 23rd, the 24th or the 25th. As I say, I fail to see a consistency of approach. I do not see why he did not deal with the words "sexual relations" when he asked about that particular day, May 22. I do not see why he did not use that same phrase "sexual relations", because he started to deal with that when he asked the corespondent this particular question; but when he particularizes he talks about another day entirely, which was four days after it was alleged that this particular event took place. The petitioner herself, when she appears as a witness, is asked, as appears on page 10:
Can you tell us something about May 22, 1959?
Then an address is mentioned, and the answer is given:
I went there. George and Rita were living there as man and wife.
The names given are the Christian names of the respondent and the corespondent. Then the witness says they were in pyjamas and indicates that certain circumstances existed. It was on May 22 that she saw these activities, yet Mr. Cohen saw fit to talk about May 26, some four days after these events were supposed to have occurred. Apart from that, we were advised about a week ago, I think, that it is most improper for counsel, at least in a court of law, to ask specific questions of that nature as to whether or not people commit adultery on a particular date. Yet Mr. Cohen disregarded that rule of the court and asked those specific questions in this instance. He fumbles them, anyway, and gets the dates wrong and backs away from the question of sexual relations and refers to these people living as man and wife on a particular day.
I submit that it should be quite acceptable, at least in this area where we are not a court of law, to admit general evidence of this kind, but if we are going to continue this practice of granting divorces through parliament, as we shall at least for a day or two- though next session, if this is not dealt with, and no one has the courage to make an announcement-

speechtext:
That was a dressed-up speech. The hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) claims that this bill of rights is not sufficiently dressed up. The simplicity of the language of this bill offends the hon. gentleman and he would like to see it dressed up in fancy language. I imagine that he could do it very nicely, too, because the hon. gentleman is very clever at that sort of thing. I am sure that if he were to draft a bill of rights it would be extremely flowery. However, that is beside the point.
The Liberal party has been quite flowery all along the line. Following the splendid

Human Rights
budget address made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) in 1958 the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Beni-dickson) rose in his place and became very flowery. He observed that the Minister of Finance was dressed in a nice blue suit with an attractive blue flower in his lapel. This apparently confused the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River somewhat so he immediately called it a blue budget. In other words, the hon. gentleman wanted to doll up the budget in the proper way with what he considered to be appropriate words.
In the budget debate in 1960 the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River made a similar attempt. There was no blue suit on that occasion to inspire him and I imagine he felt rather badly about it. I suppose he thought back to the cold porridge of his childhood so he characterized the budget with those words. That is what hon. gentlemen opposite do. They always want to doll these things up.
There is one notable exception to this rule, I refer to the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer). That hon. gentleman was talking about the cancellation of aircraft. He did not start out by being flowery at all. He could have discussed some technical shortcoming in the aircraft and said the fuselage was no good, that the proper cord was not on the upper wing or that the tail gate was not just right. Instead of that, however, the hon. gentleman said it was no ruddy good. That is the type of flowery language in which that hon. gentleman indulges.
I have very little to say about this bill. I am keenly interested in it and am proud of the fact that it was introduced by the Prime Minister on July 1. We on this side enjoy that fact very much and I know that hon. members in the opposition parties enjoy it as well. We went out on the front lawn of the parliament buildings and watched the trooping of the colour. In the evening we witnessed a parade of sea cadets. These things brought home to us the fact that these men are engaged in the defence of our nation, just as many hon. members of this house served this country well in various wars in defence of our freedom. This bill goes to the very root of our freedom.
This bill contains no small print. It is written in language everyone will be able to understand. We do not want the flowery approach at all. This bill of rights needs no special cover, no special container to sell it to thinking Canadians. It is not a piece of merchandise such as a box of candy or a bottle of scotch that needs a label trimmed with gold or a bright red ribbon around it to promote its sale. The special ingredient of value to the people of Canada is laid out

very clearly in the wording of the bill itself. Consider these words in Bill No. C-79:
An act tor the recognition and protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms.
That is plain enough for anyone to understand. I continue:
1.	This part may be cited as the Canadian bill of rights.
2.	It is hereby recognized and declared that in Canada there have always existed and shall continue to exist the following human rights and fundamental freedoms, namely,
(a)	the right of the individual to life, liberty, security of the person and enjoyment of property, and the right not to be deprived thereof except by due process of law;
(b)	the right of the individual to protection of the law without discrimination by reason of race, national origin, colour, religion or sex;
(c)	freedom of religion;
(d)	freedom of speech;
(e)	freedom of assembly and association; and
(f)	freedom of the press.
Those freedoms mean a great deal to us. I was quite interested in an article in the Ottawa Journal of June 14, 1960 entitled "Refugees Pay Big Price for Freedom". The article goes on to speak about the thousands of people that escape from communist countries whenever they can taking nothing with them. All they look for is freedom. This brings home to us the very important fact that Canada is and has been for many years a land of freedom. Some interesting and important statements have been made about freedoms. Thomas Jefferson said of the three freedoms:
Freedom of religion, freedom of the press and freedom of person under the protection of the habeas corpus, these are principles that have guided our steps through an age of revolution and reformation.
Franklin D. Roosevelt said of the freedom of religion:
Where freedom of religion has been attacked, the attack has come from sources opposed to democracy. Where democracy has been overthrown, the spirit of free worship has disappeared. And where religion and democracy have vanished, good faith and reason in international affairs have given way to strident ambition and brute force.
I will not read out the words of this bill because all hon. members know them but I will tell hon. members of the opposition that the bill needs no flowery words and no fancy package to sell it to the people of Canada because it is not for sale. It is free to all the people of Canada.

Mr. Speaker,
the previous speaker said that at five o'clock he began his speech in confusion. I am not a bit surprised at that. After listening to the remarks made by the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker) the hon. gentleman should have been confused because the minister made a speech that was extremely confusing.

Actually I know that the hon. member tor Nanaimo (Mr. Matthews) will be readily forgiven by this house because other hon. members listened to the speech made by the Minister of Public Works and I can assure hon. gentlemen that if I were one to be easily confused I, like the hon. member for Nanaimo, would have been confused as well.
The Minister of Public Works this afternoon referring to the Gettysburg address by Lincoln said it was couched in a language of great simplicity, of great purity and not in the bombastic, arrogant and pompous language which the hon. members of the opposition would suggest. I have listened to most of the speeches delivered in this house today on this bill and I know that if any speech has been made to which those adjectives could be applied it was the speech made by the Minister of Public Works.
It is not the intention of the opposition to have a bill of rights written in a bombastic, arrogant or pompous manner. I would suggest that it would be more in order if the Minister of Public Works had stated that the opposition would like to see a bill of rights written in ordinary prose that could be understood and appreciated by all the citizens of Canada and of which all the citizens could be proud. As an example, it might have gone something like this:
Her Majesty, with the Senate and House of Commons of Canada, reaffirms the fundamental rights which the dignity of man requires for every individual, not the least of which is the right to life, liberty, security of the person and the enjoyment of property.
To secure these and our other rights, governments are instituted among men, deriving their powers from the consent of the governed and their authority from the crown. It pleases Her Majesty, with her parliament in Canada, to rededicate the principle that no government ought to prejudice these rights by jeopardizing freedom of religion, freedom of speech, freedom of peaceable assembly and association, or freedom of the press.
Actually the Minister of Public Works stated this afternoon, and I quote:
But no one has suggested even in a vague form what questions could or should be asked of the supreme court-questions upon which any court could express an opinion that would assist in determining the lines of a bill of rights to be enacted by the Canadian parliament.
I think the Minister of Public Works is suffering from a short memory because Professor Bora Laskin, who is recognized as a constitutional authority, made an offer and said that he was willing to draft a question that could be submitted to the Supreme Court of Canada, and did so publicly at a meeting at which the Minister of Public Works was in attendance.
The Minister of Public Works also stated this afternoon that at the provincial-federal
Human Rights
conference in 1950 an attempt had been made to arrive at a satisfactory amending formula to overcome the necessity of going to the United Kingdom for amendments. Actually the 1950 conference was looking for a formula to eliminate the necessity of going to the United Kingdom for all amendments, not necessarily to eliminate the necessity of going to the United Kingdom to get one amendment to the British North America Act. The question submitted to the conference at that time was considerably more complicated than asking for the power to make an amendment in order to introduce a bill of rights.
I was also impressed by the Prime Minister when he introduced this bill. He said with great emphasis that he was a Canadian. It is not difficult, Mr. Speaker, to assure the house that there are 17 million people in Canada who feel exactly the same way as does the Prime Minister. I am just as proud of being a Canadian as is the Prime Minister, and I am just as anxious to have my rights respected as is the Prime Minister to have legislation so that they will be respected.

speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker.
Actually, this is not the first time that a bill of rights has been introduced in this house. On January 6, 1958 one was proposed by the opposition party and at that time the then parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Justice, the man who is now the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker), gave a great number of reasons why a bill of rights could not be introduced at that time. If I have the permission of the house I shall read part of the speech made by the Minister of Public Works who, as I said before, is suffering from a short memory, because he has entirely changed his views on a bill of rights from those which he had on January 6, 1958. Incidentally, I am about to quote from page 2892 of Hansard of January 6, 1958, in case anybody is interested:
First, should a bill be submitted to the Supreme Court of Canada and, if so, how?
In the speech that the Minister of Public Works made this afternoon he was not too concerned about this. I continue:
Should it be a draft bill, with the question asked as to whether it is within the jurisdiction of the federal parliament, keeping in mind, Mr. Speaker, that in constitutional law Canada is woefully lacking, as the hon. member I am sure will agree, in decisions on questions of this kind? In other words, where do the rights of the dominion cease under section 91 of the British North America Act and where do the rights of the provinces under section 92 begin, particularly when one discusses such abstract but very real values as freedom? Second, should we submit a series of questions to the supreme court? As my hon. friend no doubt is fully aware, to do so is very difficult because we must frame questions of law as distinct from questions of policy which latter, of course, the supreme court will not deal with.
Actually, since that time the Minister of Public Works stated it was impossible, or nobody could frame a question that could be submitted to the Supreme Court of Canada and I tell you that that is not so. I continue:
Third, should we have a parliamentary committee to explore and agree on a draft that will be suitable to parliament when it finally reaches parliament? Fourth, would it be premature to submit a draft to the supreme court and then, having their approval, come back to the house to find that it is not acceptable to hon. members, or should the government bypass the courts and reach rapport with the provinces by calling them into session, having a dominion-provincial conference on the question of a bill of rights in which

the property and civil rights of the provinces would be properly protected? Fifth, should the government itself draft a bill for the approval of and amendment by the provinces, send it to them and have them deal with it? Sixth, should we draft a strictly federal bill? Is this possible under the circumstances, in view of the property and civil rights of the provinces?
Actually this government has been in power more than three years, and during that time not a single letter went to a single province asking whether they would agree to a change or accept a formal bill of rights. The review made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker) when he presented the bill to the house was a great lesson in American history. A bill to assure civil liberties should have been based more on the experience of the commonwealth, using as its base the effectiveness of the protection of human rights in Great Britain, in Australia, in New Zealand and even in India which has had an independent government only since 1947.
In clause 2 of the bill there is mention of the right to the enjoyment of one's property. I am wondering whether that covers a person's property when it is a case of government expropriation as is now taking place in the green belt.
Subclause (d) of clause 2 refers to freedom of speech. Will that give the right to anyone to make a speech any place, any time and on any subject? Subclause (e) of clause 2 deals with freedom of assembly and association. Does this mean that public assemblies will be permitted for any purpose, at any time and in any place?
It is obviously indispensable that to protect people's rights and freedoms more than words are necessary. To this end, there should be a committee to scrutinize every order in council and regulation, as was advocated by the Prime Minister himself on November 23, 1945, and on September 22, 1949, and as quoted at some length by the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Badanai).
If the Prime Minister would study the vast experience of the commonwealth parliaments previously mentioned I know he would agree that it would be adequate, practical and desirable for every subordinate law designed to have general effect to stand referred to a scrutiny committee to be reviewed in the following respects: Whether questions of principles and policy are involved; where human rights and fundamental freedoms are affected; will it be in the power of the courts to review the validity of the subordinate laws. In this regard the scrutiny committee should have the power to report whether the order in council or regulation has any retroactive effect. The committee should report any lack of clarity. The committee should

check that all subordinate laws have been published and laid before parliament according to the Regulations Act of 1950. Finally, the committee should check whether or not regulations or orders impose a cost on public revenue or commit parliament to expenditures of any sort.
This committee should have the power to sit and to call for papers and witnesses. When I refer to witnesses I do not mean ministers because I think the place for them to give their opinions and views is in the house. The committee should have the power to report at any time. This committee should have as its adviser a highly competent parliamentary official such as the Clerk or one of his assistants or the parliamentary counsel. This type of assistance is necessary if the committee is to be effective in supervising the law-making activities of the expert and competent civil servants. We need more than words, Mr. Speaker, we need effective machinery to protect the rights of men.
