Mr. Speaker, I want to take the opportunity of this bill being introduced to say a few words.
Man can be man only so long as he is free.
This philosophical postulate could not be quoted more aptly than in the context of this discussion. Human rights are inherent to human nature. For instance the right to live and to think.
Even behind the iron curtain, the human brain cannot be prevented from thinking. In the darkest cell, the prisoner undeniably keeps his freedom of thought.
Unfortunately, in some countries, a man may not think aloud. Because he reasoned in a totalitarian state, that is in Russia, Dr. Zhivago led his author into bondage.
There is much suffering in being forgotten, but what satisfaction there is in finding the courage to express the truth after having thought and recognized it.
Mr. Speaker, thought is a divine spark. Because, if the soul is created directly by God, human intelligence is the most obvious proof that God made man in his own image. God wanted man to be free. Thus, the privileges of freedom and the rights he enjoys derive from God.
This theory having been set forth, let us put it in practice.
Canada is a country which believes in God. Its two great races have been cast in this crucible. Vast and beautiful country that it is, it has been given an appropriate motto A mari usque ad mare.
Human Rights
It is true that our country extends from the Atlantic to the Pacific; it is true that its citizens are rightly proud to belong to a young nation with a promising future.
An even greater truth is that it was the bible that inspired that motto, so inseparable are the human and supernatural aspirations of Canadians.
Various colours of the skin, different languages, various religions; those are but accidents. These are varieties in art.
While visiting our parliament, last week, General Bethouart closed his speech by saying something like this: "Let NATO follow the lead of Canada, which is so respectful of its freedoms and those of others, and success will be assured."
That was the statement of a great friend, taking the pulse of allied nations. He stops off here, and pays us that tribute.
Two days later, the right hon. Prime Minister took the floor and, in an historic speech, introduced his bill of rights. That was a noble way of celebrating Dominion day.
In Washington, tourists visiting the library of congress may stop a moment in front of a marble pedestal and read there, with respect, the American constitution.
Shortly, no doubt, visitors flocking to the Canadian parliament will stop to meditate on the declaration of rights, a bill bearing the mark of a great Canadian.
Totalitarian peoples believe in the state alone. The human person is but an individual.
Canada is a democratic country and owed it to itself to set down in this document its ideal of life, one for which men will willingly fight and lay down their lives: their freedom. In a word, I gladly support this bill.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the memory of every hon. member there are memorable events that have left an indelible mark on our lives. The present debate is one of those occasions that all of us will treasure. It will be something worth while and inspiring to hand down to the generations that follow. I suppose there are many definitions of freedom. Every individual in every separate circumstance knows, appreciates and believes in some measure of freedom. There is given to some, however, a measure of experience that lends depth, colour and substance to their appreciation of freedom.
I believe that the Prime Minister holds a unique position in that regard in this House of Commons. During the course of this debate I have been thinking back to my

Human Rights
boyhood, which was not too much different from that of a great number of Canadians who first had a taste of what freedom involved, through the expression of those things which, coming from others, told that there was a need for the recognition and protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms.
The Canadian people have not yet taken on the full stature of nationhood. Ninety-three years have not constituted sufficient time in which to fulfill the promise that was declared and held within the articles of confederation. Those who advocate a constitutional amendment would find more sympathy for their stand were it not for the fact that there is every indication that this course will remain with the Canadian people for a long period of years as an objective which nevertheless could not serve to achieve the true interests of unity and nationhood at this particular time.
Those who have ventured to criticize the language of the bill would do well to remember that it is not a constitutional amendment but rather a setting of markers within which Canadians can chart their way closer to the constitutional unity that will mark the achievement of mature nationhood. Judging by the speeches of some members of the opposition, that achievement will require a further undetermined period of time. Indeed, in listening to the hon. member for Hull (Mr. Caron), one could almost visualize that measure of immaturity, provincial outlook and ignorance in which for many years the leaders of his party were able to shelve and delay the development and achievement of those spiritual and intellectual objectives by means of which people achieve true nationhood.
On this occasion you might ask: What is freedom? My answer might be that it is the development of a personality born to fulfil the ideal of light and reason that shone in the eyes of parents who knew that the realization and fulfilment of the ideals which were the objects of their search could not be found within the land from which they came; a personality that grew with the growth of a people; a personality that grasped their problems; a personality that shared their anxieties.
July 1, 1960 will mark a triumph shared by many Canadians, with the Prime Minister of Canada. The people of Canada know, as does everyone on the government benches, who championed the supremacy of parliament. Those who sit in the opposition today also know who nurtured that right when they were the invincible majority running roughshod and arrogant, mutilating justice and freedom here in Canada. Everyone knows how that personality persevered and almost

single-handed licked that proud majority. It is one of the epics of Canadian history and it will not be forgotten by the generations to come. When the history of this parliament is written and when all other measures considered are relegated to their respective pigeonholes, this Bill No. C-79 will, in its simple forthright language, light a torch of liberty and freedom that Canadians will hold close to their bosoms whenever stress and strain test the integrity of our citizenship or the fibre of our nationhood.
In repeating the Prime Minister's closing words "I am a Canadian", the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort (Mr. Rapp) spoke as would countless Canadians were they here tonight to do so. Last night and again this morning the hon. member for Inverness-Rich-mond (Mr. MacLellan) measured our need for an assertion of recognition and protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms. His words echo the thoughts of countless Canadians today.
On this occasion when we are discussing freedom and what it means to us I wish to direct a few words to you, sir, as Speaker of this assembly. I think it fair to say that I have had occasion to look to you, Mr. Speaker, and to the chair in which you sit, with more than ordinary search and question. I should like you to know that it has been a comfort to observe how well you perform your duties. During this session I have come to have a growing reverence for the freedom that is symbolized by your position in our democracy.
On this occasion I should like to congratulate the Prime Minister first for his perseverance which kept the subject matter of this bill before the people of Canada throughout the years; second, for his eloquence and devotion which won the admiration and confidence of the Canadian people and brought them together so that this day was possible; third, because of his dedication to the cause of freedom which in Canada will ever bear the imprint of his encouragement and stature; and, finally, because he has been successful in returning to this historic party which commands the loyalty of the government benches the lighted torch that was kindled 93 years ago when the articles of confederation were in the making.

maintopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I consider it a great honour and privilege to be in the House of Commons and to be able to take part in this debate which has produced some of the finest speeches I have heard since I have been here. It is indeed only fitting that a matter as important as is the one we are discussing this evening should produce speeches of that kind.

I may say that the course of this debate has been somewhat disappointing to me because when the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) made known his intention to introduce this bill I felt it presented a rich opportunity for this parliament to make this declaration of our fundamental freedoms and human rights. Because Canada holds a special position in the world today amongst the middle nations and the emerging new nations I think that spontaneous and unanimous approval of this declaration of human rights would have had a great effect on those nations of the world today.
Almost everyone who has taken part in the debate has indicated that he feels he would like to see all the provinces participate in this bill and that it would be more valuable if this result could be brought about by a constitutional amendment which would make it enforceable in all the provinces. But that is not possible at the present time. I feel that the opposition, knowing that this is not possible at the present time, have been wrong in trying to detract from this bill.
The great value of a bill of this nature is that provision is made to protect the rights which are declared to be ours. It is important that it should have been put out with unanimous approval and brought to the attention of the public in a very forceful way to encourage all the people of this country to join in and rejoice at the passing of this bill and to encourage the provincial governments to join with us and to enact the same sort of bill in their respective legislatures.
Mr. Speaker, I feel that the opposition are trying to detract in every way they can from this measure simply by delaying the possibility of accomplishing the end we want to accomplish. I find it particularly disturbing that they should do this, because the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson), who was a member of the government which was previously in office, knows very well that some of the things he asked for cannot possibly be accomplished. Therefore he could not have had any reason to suggest them other than to try and detract from the credit which is rightfully due to the Prime Minister for introducing this bill.
I do not know what kind of consideration he wanted to be given to the bill, but in his contribution to this debate he said, as reported on page 5650 of Hansard for July 1:
This is a bill which should be submitted to a committee where witnesses could be called and where the bill could be given the same kind of consideration which this subject was given in the past when committees were set up, one of which met on 20 occasions.
I do not know whether he wants it to be given the consideration it has been given
Human Rights
in the past inasmuch as it would go off to some committee somewhere and never come back again. Perhaps that is his hope, I do not know, but it seems to me to be the kind of consideration that he would like to give it. Again I say that he could only have one reason for wanting any such consideration as that, because he would like to detract from the credit which is so rightfully due the Prime Minister for introducing this bill.
There was a rather interesting editorial in the Ottawa Journal of Monday, July 4, not referring to this debate but stating in their opinion what parliament should do with this bill. It is quite a short article and I think it is of such importance that I should take this opportunity to bring it to the attenion of the house. It is entitled "That bill of rights" and it commences:
Little in life causes more trouble than a murderous tenacity for the unattainable perfect impeding the attainable good.
That would be one of the steps which the opposition seem to suggest we should be taking, that because we cannot have everything everybody wants at one time, we should do nothing. Of course, one can appreciate that philosophy when one realizes that the Liberal government was in office for 22 years and did nothing; presumably they were operating on that philosophy throughout their tenure of office. The editorial continues:
Consider what seems to be happening in the case of Mr. Diefenbaker's bill of rights.
No one can hold sensibly that it is a bad thing for the parliament of Canada to declare at this time in favour of human rights. But simply because our political structure in Canada makes it impossible at present to make that declaration a part of Canada's constitution, some people are saying that the declaration is worthless, that it shouldn't be made at all.
Why shouldn't it be made? Surely at this time, when freedom in so many areas is under siege, it is not a bad thing for the parliament of Canada to shout its faith in freedom.
It is true that this declaration, this writ, so to speak, will not run in the provinces. But if it is ever to be made a writ that will run in our provinces, become a part of the constitution that will be enforceable, what better way of making a start towards that end than to have parliament give the lead Mr. Diefenbaker wants it to give?
This declaration of human rights should be made -be made unanimously and resoundingly.
That bears out what I have already stated to the house, because I believe that had it been given that sort of support it would have had a great deal more effect in this country and I believe every member of the house knows it would have had that effect had it received that kind of support. It would have helped Canada's position in world affairs as well as helped bring about the very ends which the opposition say they would like to bring about.

Human Rights
If there were violent differences of opinion here with matters of principle involved which the opposition could not agree to then of course one would not expect them to give that kind of support. But that is not the case with this bill of rights. I do not think that anyone in this house has indicated in any way that he is opposed to this important bill. It is the age old argument of the opposition, of course, that when the government brings in a good bill they do not dare oppose it so the only thing they can do is to try to detract from it and to say that it does not go far enough or that it should go further, and about every kind of obstacle in its way to detract from it. I suggest that is what has been done in this particular debate.
One of the main objections has been that a constitutional amendment is required. The people of Canada sent us here to legislate. They did not send us down here to re-divide the powers as between the federal and provincial governments. They sent us down here to legislate in a field open to us, namely to legislate within the power of the federal government.
I would remind the house that those same electors who sent us here are also responsible for electing the members of provincial legislatures, and if they want provincial legislatures to enact a bill of rights it will be up to these same people to instruct them to do that. That is exactly the constitutional position in the country. That is what we are sent here for and that is what we are doing at the present time.
The Prime Minister has brought this to the attention of the country many times. Throughout his parliamentary career he has fought for a bill of rights and during the election campaign the people of Canada endorsed his proposal to introduce a bill of rights. Certainly I have had many letters on this subject since I have been a member supporting the Prime Minister's proposal to bring in this bill.
I want to say I am very proud to support a bill which is brought forward in the kind of language which we have in the present bill. We have had discourses on this from very learned counsel, but I am pleased to see that it is in such language that I as a layman and every other person in Canada simply by reading this bill can see clearly set out those rights which are ours. Those rights are set out in unequivocal terms and the bill makes provision for the court to protect those rights. It states quite clearly that parliament shall not be able to infringe upon those rights without repealing the act or stating expressly that it will abridge the freedoms contained in it.
[Mr. Browne (Vancouver-Kingsway) .1
The Leader of the Opposition made one or two other observations in connection with this matter and at one point asked, "Why should people pay more attention to this bill than to previous bills?" As reported on page 5663 of Hansard for July 4 he said:
Why should a future parliament be more impressed by and respectful of this bill than it would be of historic charters of our liberties such as the Magna Carta, the petition of right of 1627, the habeas corpus act of 1640 and the bill of rights of 1689-
I suggest there is no more reason why they should be any more bound by them, but I can only say that if they pay as much attention to this bill as they paid to those, then those of us in this house at the present time who have supported this bill will certainly have every reason to be proud of ourselves for having taken part in this historic occasion. At the same time, when the course of history runs along through the coming years we will see this document taking its place in Canadian history, as have so many of these other important declarations played their part in the history of other countries. When that time comes I say that those who have opposed this bill will certainly have no right to be proud of themselves.
Therefore it gives me the greatest pleasure to be able to support the Prime Minister and the government in bringing forward this very valuable document, one which I know in the years I have been a member of parliament I will always consider to be a great privilege to have supported.

maintopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the bill placed before us today on the initiative of the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) has so far inspired a high calibre debate, in the course of which we have heard a number of interesting suggestions.
While I would not be so presumptuous as to believe that my personal intervention can be of any great help, I should like to leave with the house the results of my modest observations.
The history of civilization shows that for a long time, the pursuit and definition of human rights were mainly matters for philosophical debate and moral dissertation. Leading thinkers did perceive however-generally in a confused way-that while man, due to his nature, had to serve society, it did not follow that he should be subordinated to society in all respects, nor that society should not serve man. Christ was really the first

Human Rights
to bring us the first charter of human freedoms, summarizing in these lapidary words which after two thousand years are still amazingly timely:
Render unto Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and unto God the things that are God's.
Throughout the centuries, many battles have been waged over this principle of life. Man has never ceased to pursue the freedoms that enable him to express himself, and it may be said that for two centuries the search for and the defining of human rights have become one of the main concerns now of nations and of governments, and of both at the same time.
We learn from history that it is especially after uprisings, revolutions or social upheavals that attempts were made to define those rights in writings that were always proclaimed inalienable and permanent. Successive constitutions, in France, since 1789, have sprung from the rising of the people against the intolerance and abuse which it felt or thought it had suffered at the hands of the state authorities, or its rulers.
The first establishments which were to form New England and hold such a large place in the history of the English colonies in America, were the result of a similar feeling. For did they not originate in the landing at Plymouth Rock, on December 21, 1620? A historian eloquently remarked, and I quote:
The pilgrims who came to the New World seeking the right to pray according to their faith, brought with them neither warrant nor charter. But before they disembarked from the Mayflower, they signed the famous "pact" which contained the principles that were to rule life in their community.
Even today, Mr. Speaker, we cannot face without emotion the memory which is kept alive on the Reformation wall, in Geneva. We see, in that picture those God-fearing pilgrims, kneeling on the deck of their ship as they neared what was to be their land of freedom. Then, before separating, they sign the Mayflower pact which was to be the basis for the various subsequent establishments, that were, in a way, a prelude to the constitution of the great American democracy.
Canada, on its part, also enjoys a great heritage in this respect. Immediately after the defeat of 1760, the vanquished leaders of French Canada tried to regain its basic freedoms. The Ramezays and the De Vau-dreuils took great care, at the time of surrender, to demand as a vital need religious freedom and maintenance of our civil laws.
Article 4 of the Treaty of Paris, in 1763, was to be the first answer of the conqueror, and I quote:
79951-0-364
(Text):
His Britannick Majesty consents to grant to the inhabitants of Canada the freedom of the Catholic religion. Consequently, His Majesty will give the most effectual and precise orders so that his Roman Catholic subjects may solemnize their religion according to the rites of the Roman church in so far as the laws of Britain will allow.
(Translation):
That was an important amendment to British public law as it then existed, and I might recall incidentally, Mr. Speaker, that Canada was the chosen land where religious freedom was first recognized, even before it was recognized by the mother country for its own people.
Indeed, in 1763, as a result of the test act of 1673, no Catholic of the empire had a right to hold public office without renouncing the fundamental dogmas of his faith. The Canadian people were the first to be relieved by the act of Quebec of 1774.
Moreover, Mr. Speaker, when we look at that part of our history, we can say that Canada was the first country where for the first time since Henry VIII recognition was given to the rights and freedoms belonging not only to Catholics but to all religious denominations. Thus, this act of Quebec was followed in England by the Roman Catholic relief act of 1829, following the fights waged by O'Connell. This act of Quebec came some fifty years before the conquest of religious freedom in the United Kingdom. In Canada, this conquest went on when the Jews, then living in England in semi-freedom, were granted here, as early as 1832, a status recognizing their religious freedom. It was the same for Protestants and dissenters, until 1852 when during the period of union act, the first act was passed definitely and absolutely acknowledging freedom for all sects and religions then known in Canada.
That is the heritage we are still enjoying today, a rich and valuable heritage which enables us more than any other nation perhaps to rank among the first countries seeking to have recognized in specific, precise and definite terms, the fundamental freedoms that all men hope for and which allow fulfilment of their personality.
Canada could not show unconcern about this heritage when on December 10, 1948, after three years of discussions, of debates and planning, the general assembly of the United Nations passed a measure of 30 items covering a number of human rights of various nature, the recognition of which, in the opinion of the assembly itself, was the basis of world freedom, justice and peace.

Human Rights
That universal statement on human rights was soon to operate. Thus, all the texts of constitutions set up since, all basic legislation and laws of newly formed states, or of countries rising from their ruins, as well as the various agencies of the United Nations, international treaties and agreements, the judgments and views of international courts of justice and even of some national courts have been impregnated by that statement and are a proof of its deep influence on world opinion today.
Having signed that document, Canada could hardly ignore the moral obligation thus assumed. Therefore, the present Prime Minister submitted that serious issue to the House of Commons as early as in 1948.
During the 1950 session, the Senate set up a committee which was to investigate the facts and submit its conclusions. That report, which was published on June 27 of that year, recommended that human rightsbased on equality before the law and public order-
-be confirmed by a solemn statement.
Many times since the problem has been the subject matter of eloquent debate until the 1958 session, when the Prime Minister of Canada took the leadership in this field and gave it the form of a bill, which was then deliberately shelved to give Canadians time to consider it and to express their views. That bill is today before us.
And what, essentially, does it consist of?
In his treaty on constitutional law and political institutions the prominent columnist of Le Monde, Mr. Maurice Duverger, stated that:
The limitation of government action through the recognition of a citizen's political freedoms works on two levels.
On the one hand, freedoms serve to define an area that is closed to government activity, an area for private action, reserved to the individual; on the other hand, within the very area that is open to government activity, freedoms provide means of opposing the government, means of preventing the government from wielding too much power.
The text before us, largely based on the universal declaration of human rights, is clearly directed to this double purpose. Thus, after recalling man's right to life, liberty, security and the enjoyment of property, without discrimination as to race, national origin, colour, religion or sex, it expressly proclaims freedom of religion, freedom of speech, freedom of the press, freedom of assembly and association. Then there are protective provisions against arbitrary detention or imprisonment, something which
[Mr. Dorion.l
recalls and reemphasizes the great British legal institutions which, since the conquest, have become an integral part of our common heritage.
Since its publication this bill has been taken apart and commented upon by many politicians, lawyers and sociologists. Some have regretted its formal inadequacy and the lack of any criminal penalties; others- and I think that is the purpose of the amendment now before us-feel that, instead of passing a mere federal law, we should proceed to amend the constitution so that each and every province would be subject to its provisions.
Any legislation, however important, must strictly take into account the structure of the legislating government. Canada is a federation. Our constitution provides for a distribution of powers and responsibilities as between the federal government and the provincial governments, both of which are sovereign in their particular field.
The result is that some sections of the declaration drafted by the United Nations cannot be incorporated into a federal legislation without constituting an infringement upon the legislative autonomy of the provinces. I think that, during the debate at United Nations, it was the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) himself who pointed out that danger.
A bill of rights that would begin by violating the constitution which Canadians have accepted, and which ensures the fulfillment of their personality, would appear as a bold stroke of striking inconsistency.
Would it be better to amend the constitution? Perhaps, but then the amending procedure would have to be provided by the constitution itself, or else accepted by all provinces. Now, no such procedure has been provided in the act of 1867, and most amendments to the act since were introduced exclusively by the federal government, without the active support of the provinces, even if, at times, there was prior consultation. In such a delicate matter, the amending procedure would barely disguise the abuse of power of which, in fact, the federal government would become guilty. What respect could we have for a text drafted, if not in formal illegality, at least in illegitimacy?
Others find the Prime Minister's project inadequate and, in some respects, laconic. Of course, clearly discernible is the desire not to impinge upon powers beyond the jurisdiction of the federal state. That, in my opinion, does not in the least detract from

its value; on the contrary, it is all to the credit of the Prime Minister, and he deserves our congratulations for it. The draft is couched in simple terms, that everybody can understand, and it avoids anything that could give rise to violent controversy.
As General Lafayette said in the French constituent assembly, the character of such a declaration consists in truth and precision: it must recite what everyone knows, what everyone wants. It must state only indisputable principles, only morally and legally indefeasible rights inherent to all systems, since the rights it purports to proclaim are natural rights that are vital to man and his development at all times and in all countries.
But what about the lack of penal sanction? Much could be said on that score, but my time is running out. Let me point out that this objection does not take into account the nature and true purpose of the document. In his Christmas message of 1940, His Holiness Pope Pius XII precisely urged nations to proclaim a universal declaration of rights and to transpose it into their own legislation; he defined the character of such a declaration and pointed out its ultimate purpose in those terms:
To calm the agitation and bitterness of all those who feel threatened or injured In their existence or deprived of the free exercise of their activity.
Published not just by philosophers or moralists, but by legislators and public administrators, such statements become in the hands of men, and by the sole power of their verity, instruments of protection and defence before the courts and public opinion. They help fight injustice and arbitrary decisions. Moreover, at the same time, they teach man the moral obligations that also involve the respect of another man's property. In a country such as this, where two races with different origins, cultures and beliefs live side by side, a bill of rights will help bring those races closer together, help shape public opinion, cause the great law of Christian charity to become deeply rooted in the soul of everyone and finally provide for French speaking Canadians and English speaking Canadians equal rights and freedoms in all and every part of our wide and beautiful country.

maintopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have all listened to the debates with a great deal of interest and I believe we have all learned something from what has been said. It would appear that a bill of rights means many things to many people, and not the same thing to each individual.
79951-0-364J
Human Rights
It seems to me that we are putting a great deal of faith in a bill that is as simply written and as fundamental as this bill of rights appears to be. It will be true, as the hon. member for Russell (Mr. Tardif) said a few moments ago, that the lawyers will interpret it as they see fit, and many applications will come from a very humble beginning.
For many years the Canadian people have been told that they need a bill of rights and that a bill of rights is a good thing. I wonder how much we really needed a written bill of rights? I wonder whether this bill of rights which outlines certain liberties of the Canadian people will actually limit them by enumerating them? Will it not to some extent limit federal jurisdiction, and particularly the jurisdiction of the courts which have served well the English people, Canadians and others who have taken their cases before them, and finally in many instances to the highest courts of the land?
I keep thinking that the Roncarelli case was a very good example. While we may argue that it cost a lot of money to carry it through the courts-it took seven years-I think it is generally agreed that the Canadian people achieved from the courts in the end a sense of fair play and an indication of what justice was.
I am inclined to believe that quite often when we pass a statute, when we introduce a bill that limits by its scope many things by enumerating exactly what it will protect, we put ourselves in this position. Many of the things that are not mentioned, many of the things that are not considered to be rights today will be debated and will become court cases in the future because provincial governments may well decide that they are within their jurisdiction because those matters which come within the jurisdiction of the federal government are enumerated in this legislation.
I listened very carefully to the arguments put forward on behalf of a bill of rights that would be suitable to teach to the growing generation and would give them probably as great a sense of nationalism as does the constitution of the United States, the story of George Washington and the cherry tree and so forth. I believe there is some merit in this suggestion. I would think the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) should give consideration to including a preamble that could be brought to the attention of our children, something which would give them a sense of Canadian-ism and of ownership of those rights that we are now enumerating. I am sure that

Human Rights
many of our children if they were given the bill of rights we have before us would find very little in it that is not in other legal documents.
The constitutional aspects of whether we should have a bill of rights in our constitution or whether it should be an act of parliament which could be changed by subsequent governments is worthy of a great deal of consideration. We should feel in Canada that no matter what province one comes from he has equal rights with the people in other provinces. Obviously this can only be accomplished by putting it in a constitution which cannot be changed at the whim of either a federal government or any particular provincial government. I do not think we need to enumerate the cases that in recent years have shown the need for those rights to be granted in provincial fields. I refer to the right of assembly which is given to the unions, which can be taken away in certain provinces and yet is generally accepted and is on the statute books of the federal government. This right is given to all citizens under federal jurisdiction. In this field we have rights and liberties of the Canadian people that we have come to accept. Therefore, I think there is something to be said for putting this into stronger form than a simple act of the House of Commons.
On the other hand, Mr. Speaker, there is something to be said for having a bill in this form. It would appear to me that the bill of rights that the Canadian people will get will depend entirely on the attitude of the people themselves and their interpretation of it. I would suggest that as we grow up in this country and throughout the world and as we enlarge our concept of what liberty is we shall before too long want to write into a bill of rights the right of freedom from want. We shall be interested in adding economic implications to it so that no people in this country will be in want of food and the basic necessities of life.
It will not be too long before we shall want to put in a bill of rights certain rights with regard to our health structure so that Canadians at all times any place in Canada will be entitled to reasonable and extensive care as they may need it.
If the bill of rights is in such a form that it can be maintained by subsequent governments we shall be surprised in 25 or 50 years at just how many things the Canadian people have assumed for themselves as fundamental rights, and they will not be as basic as the rights outlined in this particular bill. In my opinion this means that the bill of rights will mean only what the government of the day wants it to mean. If we have governments such as we have had in various provinces of

Canada which do not believe in freedom of the press, then there will be no freedom of the press. If we have governments which do not believe in the right of assembly, then there will be no right of assembly, and we have seen this happen in some of the provinces. If we believe in freedom of religion, then we will have freedom of religion with this bill or with the interpretation that we get from our courts. We have seen in provinces where they do not believe in freedom of religion that we did not have that right and this bill of rights will not make any difference to them.
We are going to have a federal-provincial conference on July 25. I would suggest that the Prime Minister hold off his bill of rights until that time and then present it to the premiers of the provinces. I would be surprised if there are not a number of the provinces which, without any preliminary work being done, without any discussions, will agree to accept this bill of rights and recommend that it be strengthened and that other liberties be put into it at the same time. I am also quite sure there are a number of provinces in this country which will not agree to accept the bill of rights and make it a constitutional amendment. We have an obligation to those who will not accept a bill of rights at this time to continually keep bringing this matter to the premiers of those provinces and to the people of those provinces until we have educated them at least into accepting what I would consider to be a very basic set of principles.
I believe that a bill of rights will be only as good as the government that is administering it. I have no doubts about this government and certainly about the Prime Minister of this country administering a bill of rights so that it will mean anything to a great number of people. If a bill of rights is going to mean anything it is going to have to take into consideration two parties. It is going to have to mean something to the individual and it is going to have to mean something to the crown at least. Those two parties are going to be involved every time the question of the bill of rights comes before the people.
The individual is going to be concerned and the crown must be concerned. Yet in this bill we do not have a very simple clause saying that the crown will be bound by this legislation as well as the individual. We do not have such a clause in this bill although it is found in most of our acts. It is a clause that is necessary at all times in order to bind the crown. It is to be found in the Interpretation Act. Such a clause could easily have been added at the end of this bill in order to make the crown also a responsible

party with respect to any action taking place under the bill of rights. The bill provides freedom for the individual but does not place any restraint on the other party, the crown. I suggest that at least with respect to federal matters the crown must be a party to the bill.
I rose on a point of order the other day, Mr. Speaker, and tried to indicate that already at this session we have passed at least one bill containing clauses which eliminate the benefits to be gained from the bill of rights. The Feeds Act is very simple legislation, but in 11 instances in that act we have eliminated rights that the Canadian people have come to assume are theirs. We have eliminated security of property through the right to search without a warrant. We have eliminated protection against self-incrimination. We have removed the protection against forced confessions. Excessive fines are provided which involve cruel and inhuman punishment. We have provided in this bill for arbitrary detention affecting the liberty of the person. We have eliminated the right to interference by counsel. We have eliminated the right not to be deprived of the enjoyment of property without due process of law. The right to a fair hearing has been abrogated. The right of the accused to confront crown witnesses and cross-examine has been eliminated. The right of the accused to stand trial where the offence occurs has been eliminated.
This was all done in one simple bill we passed this year. I make no apology for not having risen and saying something about the matter at that time. Frankly I did not know anything about it. This is an argument that can only be developed by lawyers, and as it was pointed out to me I am quite happy to point out the effect of that legislation. I have read the arguments and have studied the bill and out of the eleven instances that legal counsel have put forward I can find seven or eight myself and I am only a common, ordinary person.
Nobody questions the legal ability of the Prime Minister. He controls the government. We do not have control by a 25-man cabinet but rather government by an individual. It is his government and it will rise and fall with him. In my opinion he has the capabilities necessary to decide these matters. I will feel quite secure about his bill of rights and will be happy to say I have been wrong if I find that in the next week or two he withdraws the Feeds Act or eliminates those provisions of that act to which I have referred.
I have used the Feeds Act as an example not because it is the worst one but because
Human Rights
it was passed at this session and therefore fits my argument. There are other acts of the same kind. Take, for example, the Fisheries Act. Under that act an inspector can be a political appointee. As a political appointee he can seize a boat because he has reason to believe that something is not cricket with respect to the operation of the boat. He can hold the boat and then turn it back to the fisherman and say, "Thank you, I did not have any grounds; there is your boat and you can do what you like with it." The fisherman has no redress. The inspectors are protected under the act. All I suggest is that if the bill of rights means as much as some of the backbenchers seem to think it means then I am sure the government will immediately withdraw all legislation containing arbitrary powers eliminating the right to counsel and the right to protection against having to make confessions that may incriminate.
When these powers are eliminated I will believe that the Prime Minister is sincere in bringing forward a bill of rights, a bill that does not affect all the Canadian people but only those who are affected by acts passed under the jurisdiction of the federal parliament. In my opinion this measure will in no way interfere with the rights of the provincial governments.
I could go on and mention some of the things that I do not like that are happening in the immigration department, the fact that the mounted police have made raids in the middle of the night and assaulted men and women and this on the Indians that we keep on reservations we have set apart for them. I could point out these things but I do not think it would do any good because they are things that have happened in the past and we do not want to say anything about them. But I would suggest that if the members of the government are sincere in their belief, and I think they are, they have an obligation to start immediately to check all legislation we have passed in the last three or four years at least and to see that our legislation will give the people the rights we want them to have and are promising them in the bill of rights.
When that is done then in my opinion we in Canada will be able to write for ourselves a preamble to the bill of rights in concise and flowery language, even as flowery as the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) would like it to be, which will mean something to our school children. We can dress up the bill of rights so that every school child can learn about these rights and will feel proud of being a Canadian. They will know they have those rights we now have

Human Rights
through British law. As it is now, when we go to court one lawyer will get up and say that we have these rights and another lawyer will get up and say we have not. Then you look in your pocket and if you have enough money you hire the best lawyer. He says you have them and you win the case and you get off.
I am told that the Roncarelli case was before the courts for seven years and in many instances the justice handed out in that case was a disgrace to the Canadian people. We all agree that a fair and just decision was rendered when the case finally went to the Supreme Court of Canada. But such a result can only be achieved by the rich and will not accrue to the poor. The things that were spoken about this afternoon in such a flowery way were not given to the rich in England or the United States. They were given in the main to the poor people, to the people who could not afford to fight for themselves. Most of those rights were granted not after a revolution or an upset in the country but because of decisions by people like our supreme court judges who sat back in their little ivory towers and decided that this was right and that it should be given to the people.
We want to have a bill of rights in Canada. I have wanted a bill of rights for a long time. I agree with those who have said that they want the bill of rights to be simple so that Canadians can understand it. This bill of rights is simple and it can be a good bill of rights. It can be as good a bill of rights as the government that is going to administer it wishes to make it but if the government will not take action to eliminate those things that are provided to the contrary by other legislation of the federal government then I do not think the bill of rights will be worth the paper it is written on.
I think that in the next few months the Canadian people are going to be watching to see what happens with respect to the legislation with which they come in contact. The little fisherman who has some gear in a boat is going to be interested if his boat is seized by an inspector and no charge is laid and there is no right to prosecute the inspector. The feed mill owner will be interested when he calls in his lawyer and finds that the lawyer not only cannot have a privileged communication with his client but becomes a second party who can be questioned and has to give evidence under penalty of a fine himself.
If the little people across the country who are affected by the acts of the federal government find that these acts have been liberalized and find that what the Prime Minister said about the bill of rights was

not idle talk but was talk that was going to apply to them, then they will remember John Diefenbaker and his bill of rights for a long time. But if they continually find that those acts are abused and that the bill of rights is being invoked against other federal acts, they are going to question whether he was honest in his interpretation of applying this to all the Canadian people.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of ihe Opposition):
maintopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the vote on the amendment is taken I think it is desirable that I should explain the position we will take with regard to it. The amendment reads as follows:
That this bill be not now read a second time, but be it resolved that this house is of the opinion that the provinces should be consulted in order to ascertain whether agreement can be reached on the terms of a constitutional amendment to guarantee human rights and fundamental freedoms.
So far as the amendment deals with the desirability of consultation with the provinces, we on this side of the house have advocated that consultation during this debate and indeed on various occasions when we were dealing with this subject. We therefore naturally support the idea of consultation with the provinces so that out of that consultation there may develop in one form or another, with provincial agreement-because that is the only way in which it can be done-a bill of rights which will cover all Canadians and all subjects whether they are under provincial jurisdiction and federal jurisdiction.
This afternoon the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker) in his intervention in this debate stated that the previous government during its years of office had done nothing to promote consultation with the provinces in these matters. I would remind him that he himself mentioned the constitutional conference of 1950 which was at least an effort to bring about agreement with the provinces so that when action had to be taken in matters of this kind, which required a constitutional amendment before that action could cover the whole of the country, arrangements could be made for that to be done by some amending procedure in our own country.
The minister talked about the abortive nature of that conference. May I say this, Mr. Speaker. That conference represented at least an effort to make progress in this direction. While it did not accomplish everything the government of that day had in mind, that conference accomplished this result. It made possible the amendment of the Canadian constitution by Canadian action, without reference to any other outside jurisdiction, in respect of all those matters under federal jurisdiction. That achievement represented progress. Because of the action taken at that

time in 1950 this government today, if it had so desired, could have introduced this bill in the form of a constitutional amendment. As has been pointed out by the Prime Minister and others, this bill deals only with matters under the jurisdiction of the federal parliament. Hence because of the action which was taken in 1950 the government could have made this bill, as far as its contents are concerned, a matter for constitutional amendment by action of this parliament and not action of any other parliament at any time.
The Prime Minister has said that was not done because it was not really important to have it done in that way because a constitutional amendment of that kind can be altered in the same way in which it can be made, namely by action of this parliament. But as I pointed out on Monday, that surely is a strange argument and one which depreciates the importance of having something in our constitution. If the principle of this bill is so important as it has been stated to be by so many hon. members on the other side who have spoken; if it is indeed a landmark in our history; if it is indeed a Canadian Magna Carta, might it not have been wise to have brought this matter before this house in the form of a constitutional amendment covering federal matters alone so that it at least would have the sanctity of enshrinement in our constitution? That was not done but it could have been done because of the action taken in 1950.
This amendment goes beyond that point. This amendment deals with consultation in order to ascertain whether we can have the kind of bill of rights or bills of rights, if we need more than one, which would cover all subjects under all the jurisdictions and therefore cover all Canadians. As I have said, we of course support this idea of consultation. But what has the present government-which will be faced with this amendment as we are faced with it-done with regard to bringing about this kind of consultation?
The Prime Minister and others have pointed out that it is idle to talk about consultation with a view to bringing about a wider bill of rights because it is obvious that such consultation will lead to nothing but delay. Our quarrel with the government on this matter is that no effort of any kind has been made in nearly three years by the government to find out whether this pessimistic prediction is in fact the case. It is quite true that if in the future as little effort is made to bring about this kind of consultation with the provinces as has been made in the last two and a half years this amendment would indeed result in indefinite delay for any bill
Human Rights
of rights of any kind. The record of the past shows that we are not likely to have, unless that record is changed, the kind of consultation which is needed and which might, despite the pessimistic predictions made, result in agreement.
It has been pointed out by more than one speaker on this side of the house that there are already two provincial bills of rights. The new premier of the province of Quebec who has just been installed in office has already declared that he is in favour of a provincial bill of rights. Has any province come out against the idea of a bill of rights or a declaration of rights or a federal bill of rights, with the same kind of bill introduced in the provinces? Has any province come out against that in principle in the last two and a half years? Has any province discouraged initiative by the federal government which might have brought that about by now? Not to my knowledge, Mr. Speaker. Nevertheless the government has done nothing about it at all except to say that consultation is idle and delaying, that nothing can be expected from it and therefore they will bring this bill of rights forward as an ordinary bill of rights, not even as a constitutional measure covering federal matters alone. Hence that part of the amendment dealing with the consultation side of the question does not present the opposition with any difficulty.
But, Mr. Speaker, the real significance of this amendment, of course, lies in the first line:
That this bill be not now read a second time,-
That phraseology, makes the amendment a purely negative one. Not only is it negative in that sense technically but it rejects the principle embodied in this bill. The expression "that this bill be not now read the second time" would be killing the bill on second reading when we are dealing with the principle of the bill.
Mr. Speaker, we on this side have already said we would support the principle of this bill, but we wish that principle to be implemented more effectively. Having taken that position, how could we then vote for an amendment the effect of which is to kill the bill and negative the principle of the bill? What we want to see done, now that this bill has been introduced, even in the form in which it has been introduced, inadequate though it may be for the purposes we all hope to achieve, is to see the bill passed in second reading and sent to a committee.
We would have liked to have seen the promise made by the Prime Minister (Mr. HOUSE OF COMMONS
Human Rights
Diefenbaker) of this country to the bar association at its annual convention in Vancouver last September carried out, the promise by which a bill of rights "in the early days of next session", that is, the present session, would have been sent to a joint committee of the House of Commons and the Senate at which evidence could have been heard from those interested in giving such evidence, including the bar association itself.
As I pointed out the other day, that specific commitment given with definite assurance by the Prime Minister resulted in the bar association passing in one of its committees a resolution which said that it would be possible to discuss this matter in this joint parliamentary committee and therefore they would reserve their opinion until they had the chance to appear before it. That cannot be done as proposed. Perhaps we are not yet at the end of the session but we are certainly not in the early days of it. All we can do now is to get this bill as soon as we can to a committee, perhaps even at this stage- I do not know what the intentions of the government are-to a joint committee. But at least we can get a committee set up and can summon to the committee witnesses, organizations, individuals and experts. Some of the witnesses and some of the organizations have been waiting for two years to appear before such a committee.
If because this is the middle of July it is not going to be possible to get all the witnesses before the committee demanded by the seriousness of the subject, that will not be our responsibility. But we will do our best to make this committee work. We will do our best to help secure witnesses before this committee. We have already suggested in this debate certain concrete changes which can be made, we think with advantage, to this bill. We will have an opportunity, I hope, to bring these changes to the attention of the committee.
Incidentally in the course of this discussion some very thoughtful speeches have been made on all sides of the house, but we have not heard very much from the government side about the proposals we on this side have made in the hope that they would improve the bill and make it a better bill when it comes out of committee, back to this house during this session later in the summer; and when the house in committee of the whole will have a chance to go over the work of the committee, examine the changes which have been made, and perhaps pass a bill before the session is over which will really implement in an effective and impressive way the purposes which we all have in mind when we discuss human rights and fundamental freedoms.

We cannot do any of that if this amendment carries, because if it carries it kills the bill. That is the purpose of the amendment.

Mr. Speaker, when this matter came up last year I had the pleasure of attending a lecture delivered by Professor A. M. Lower at the University of Ottawa. As everyone knows, Professor Lower is the very distinguished author of a history text book which is standard in most universities entitled, "Colony to Nation", and as most people know he is no great or abiding friend of the government or of the party to which I belong. His book "Colony to Nation" is written in a very racy and ingratiating style. However, one should not take it too seriously because it presents the Liberal or authorized version of Canadian history. I think it is very fortunate that we have people like Professor Creighton who can set the record straight. However, I must admit that Mr. Lower could not restrain a sneaking respect for the founder of the Conservative party and original prime minister of Canada, the late Sir John A. Macdonald.
But I was very gratified and pleased at the support that Mr. Lower gave for a bill of rights. I was fortunate enough to have the pleasure of meeting him afterwards and he was kind enough to give me the verbatim notes of his speech. There are several passages I should like to quote directly from his speech because I think they are extremely material to the discussion tonight. I quote from Professor Lower's remarks:
I agree wholeheartedly that the present administration is sincerely anxious to increase the guarantees of Canadian freedom. The problem is too big to be allowed to become merely a matter of ordinary party bickering. Those who try to make it merely a party matter will do their country no service.
He went on to say:
I recognize the weaknesses of a simple statute instead of a constitutional amendment, but I recognize the impossibility of getting this latter at the present time. A half loaf is better than no bread. If I were an M.P., I would call for drastic

Human Rights
revision and strengthening of that part of the bill dealing with the War Measures Act, and would cheerfully vote for the rest of it.
Professor Lower stated that if he were a member of parliament he would call for a strengthening of the war measures provisions and would cheerfully vote for the rest of the bill. He stated further:
I hope all Canadians will have gumption enough to see in the gesture of the present government concern for their liberties.
He stated something else that is very material and which I should like to put on the record because he expresses it in a most succinct and intelligent manner. He said:
Our bill of rights will touch on the subject of civil liberties, not on civil rights at all, and, as such, I suspect it will affect the whole country. It will be a great statement of principle. It will be comparable to the American declaration of independence.
I quote further:
If you want another parallel for the statement of principles, I can think of a very pertinent one which nobody here will repudiate, that is to say, the innumerable statements of principles which we find stated in the holy writ. I suppose there are very few people who have not consciously or unconsciously, at some time or other, violated the precepts that are laid down for us in the scriptures but somehow, these precepts have a way of bringing us back to them. We take the simple case of the ten commandments. One of them states: "Thou shalt not steal", yet there is a great deal of theft in the world. Nevertheless, we come back to the principle and it has been so strong and so powerful a principle that it is upheld by the secular law of the land. My point is that, if you enunciate a great principle, which is intrinsically sound, sooner or later, your law will be shaped accordingly; and sooner or later he will begin to think accordingly too.
I could not agree more with this direct verbatim quotation from Professor Lower. I am glad to say that there is one instance in which I can thoroughly agree with him.
For many years prior to the last two great wars many people had the idea of the inevitable march of freedom. It used to be taken for granted or it was assumed that by some natural law one nation after another would introduce some form of representative government modelled on the mother of parliaments and that in due course freedom would become universal. To me this is just another of those liberal illusions-that is liberal with a small "1"-that was initiated by the French revolution. It is in the same category as is this faith in the inevitable progress and the ultimate perfectability of man. These two illusions are one thing that Liberals, communists, socialists and so on have in common, namely this naive faith which is founded on a misconception of human nature.
Conservatives, basing their feeling on an older and more orthodox Christian tradition,

realize that human egotism must be restrained by good laws and that human altruism will always be bolstered by sound institutions. They also realize that there is no guarantee of any inevitable progress. In human history we go forward and we go backward. There is always in human history the possibility of human creativity and destructivity.
Unfortunately, as I have stated, this optimism that freedom was inevitable has not been justified by events. Our democratic form of government has gone entirely out of fashion and has been replaced in many countries by the rule of a dictator or a tyrannical clique. Even in Canada our rulers seem to have been attracted by the illusion of the efficiency of government wartime controls and to have become impatient with the relatively slower and more pedestrian processes of democracy. It has been the evidence of this which has led thinking men to advocate clear-cut legislation to guarantee personal liberty in place of our vague traditions.
It is evident that this bill should have been introduced by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) because his efforts to secure such legislation go back for a long time. He raised the matter in 1942. In 1947 he made a speech in parliament which aroused great interest in the subject of a bill of rights not only in Canada but in the United Nations. On many occasions between 1947 and the defeat of the previous government the Prime Minister raised his voice to urge on an unsympathetic house the passing of just such a bill as that which is before us. As Prime Minister he has drafted the bill of rights; and in order that it should receive the fullest consideration and study he introduced the bill and had it given first reading last September and then let it stand over until this present session.
In 1945, when the charter of the United Nations was drawn up in San Francisco, proposals were already being made that an international bill of human rights should be drafted. This first international declaration of human rights was adopted without a single dissenting vote. It consisted of 26 articles and covered a very wide range of personal, civic, political, economic and other types of rights.
Those 26 articles did not have the force of binding rules of law either in international relations or in the domestic law of any of the states which approved them but they represent the aspirations of the common men and women of this age. They are a statement of what ought to be. They represent a challenge and a goal, and in most parts of the world that goal is tragically far removed from actual conditions. It is the old story of

the tragic disparity between our aims and our achievements. However, the United Nations declaration of human rights is an inspiration to us as well as to others and it forms the background to the fight which the Prime Minister has been waging for a bill of rights in Canada.
Since no one in Canada would ever admit that he was opposed to freedom, it seems surprising that opposition members, or some of them, would have in the past rejected the Prime Minister's arguments. However, a bill of rights meant a curb to the power of the previous government which, incidentally, it was by no means ready to accept. Among the members who opposed this suggestion of a bill of rights on numerous occasions was the late Mr. Garson, the former minister of justice. I quote from his speech in the House of Commons where on one occasion he stated as follows:
The introduction of this deceptively simple but rather emotional issue into such a complex field creates a problem which is an extremely difficult one. It is the problem of superimposing a bill of rights, after the United States fashion, upon the federal constitution of Canada, whose main feature, inherited from the constitution of Great Britain, is the sovereignty of its legislative bodies ... It is this British principle which the hon. member for Prince Albert proposes to abridge by attaching constitutional limitations to it in the manner of the bill of rights in the United States constitution.
Mr. Garson, of course, was obviously referring to the fact that the parliament of Britain is completely unfettered. It has the power to confiscate your home, to imprison you or to do anything. In fact, it is a cliche in law circles that the only thing the British parliament cannot do is to change a man into a woman. In contrast, under the United States system of government we know that the first ten sections of the United States constitution provide a bill of rights to which all legislation must be subject.
It should be remembered, of course, that this absolute and unfettered power possessed by the British parliament is not due to any deliberate planning but is due to the fact that parliament has gradually acquired the power originally possessed by despotic kings who knew no bounds to their power save the limits placed on tyranny by the threat of rebellion. This accident of history has left the British parliament with a constitution resting on usage which knows no restraint on its legislative power. Because the tyrannical government of Charles I and James II provoked rebellions which led to the termination of their kingly jobs and in one instance the termination of life we are prone to think of government tyranny as related only to monarchy. I am sure that those who have
Human Rights
the responsibility of directing affairs at Westminster do not make that mistake. They know that stubborn Englishmen who have grown up with traditions of liberty and independence can be pushed only so far and that they will accept despotic regimentation no more readily from some bureaucrat than they will from a monarch and they have learned not to risk such an explosion.
But our population is like that of the United States. It is composed of many elements. Our history in some respects is similar to that of the United States. We have this tradition of violence. We are not a homogeneous people who have lived in isolation for a thousand years so that we should develop our own way of life and our own traditions.
Many people in both the United States and Canada came from countries where the common man was not encouraged to talk back to officials and where there was no traditional liberty. Even those of Anglo-Saxon origin have lost that stubborn, rebellious spirit. Let me say to the English "Be not proud". Let them know that this Magna Carta they boast of was actually promises extracted by French knights and French barons from a French king. Let them realize also that the language of the English courts for 300 years after Magna Carta was the language of France. Let them also realize before they become too proud that the greatest judge who ever adorned the English bench was not an Englishman but a Scotsman, Lord Mansfield.
As for the previous government which was in office, men like Mr. Howe and Mr. Garson, who shared with other members of the cabinet the odium of stifling the discussion of the pipe line contract, also appeared eager to abuse their great powers. Mr. Howe, Mr. Garson and the rest have had their day and will never play the tyrant again. But there are those in power who suffer from illusions of grandeur and there are many who think that some legal restraints should be applied to keep anybody who in future endeavours to emulate them within bounds.
Many well-intentioned people who support the concept of a bill of rights are of the opinion that there should be a constitutional amendment. I am not too sure-and I throw this out because I certainly make no pretensions to being a constitutional lawyer-that this bill of rights as it stands would not apply directly to the provinces. The property and civil rights reserved under section 92 of the British North America Act to the provinces refer to quite a different thing. That is property and civil rights. It is a translation from an old French legal term, "proprietes et droits civils". That was a well known phrase long before the English conquest. It

Human Rights
was put in that section by Sir George Etienne Cartier, and of course was designed to safeguard the customary laws of the province of Quebec; for example, the family law, the rights to inheritance and that sort of thing. It had nothing whatever to do with civil liberties, which is a different matter and which could more correctly be called public laws.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) has decided not to seek such an amendment because of the question of delay. He obviously arrived at the same conclusion as Professor Lower. That half a loaf of bread is better than none. He stated on one occasion:
In so far as constitutional amendment would be concerned, the experience of 80 years indicates very clearly that the provinces, jealous of their jurisdiction, would not support a constitutional amendment applicable to themselves.
