maintopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext: Order. I wonder if the hon. member would agree with me that the vote which has been taken has pretty well disposed of the question of a constitutional amendment and that we might confine ourselves now to the bill before the house.

maintopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker.
In closing, there are others who might say that this is just a simple statute. If it can be passed by a government it can be repealed by a government. This is literally true, but can you imagine the outcry which would be created if any government presumed to do such a thing? What government would dare repeal a statute which guaranteed our civil liberties? Anyone who considers the matter will acknowledge that the Prime Minister is right in saying that if this bill is passed no government will ever dare repeal it.
Finally, nothing would be more appropriate than to refer again to the initiator of the bill and to one of his statements or promises. The Prime Minister said:
Henceforth, except within the limitations that security demands, Canadians will know that their rights are not to be loosely disregarded, and parliament will have before it at all times the warning which is emphasized in this bill of rights, namely that fundamental rights and freedoms within the federal jurisdiction shall not be made light of by this or future parliaments.
I would extend that also to the provinces, either legally or by precept, that within the federal jurisdiction fundamental rights and freedoms shall not be made light of by this or future parliaments.

maintopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I feel that history is being made here in this debate on the bill of rights and it is a great privilege to have an opportunity of having a seat in this house on this historic occasion.

During the debate many views have been expressed by various members. I think all the views have been expressed which could possibly be expressed and all the avenues of approach have been explored. Therefore I do not intend to speak at any length at all. I merely want to congratulate the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) on having realized the dream of many years when he introduced this bill. I want to congratulate him on the language of the bill, which I consider is very clear and very plain and simple, and thus very eloquent. It is language which can be readily understood by the layman as well as by the professional man.
When one aspires to be the Prime Minister of Canada I believe he must have in mind greater aims and objectives than just the mere holding of the office of Prime Minister. I think our present Prime Minister is justified in holding the great office of Prime Minister because of this one aim alone, although he has many aims and objectives.
This bill has been exposed to much criticism and also approval both inside and outside the house. It is quite obvious it is impossible to please everyone. It is impossible to draw up a bill in a form which will express everybody's ideas as to how a bill should be prepared. The main thing is that we need a bill of rights in Canada and we need one now.
Mr. Speaker, like Her Majesty's loyal opposition I am going to support this bill, but unlike them I am going to be consistent and speak in favour of it too. From the remarks I have heard them make this evening and during this debate I can only infer that they are just trying to justify their own inaction in regard to a bill of rights when they had the opportunity to bring one in while they were in office.
I believe it is very important that we should watch very carefully, especially in these days when government is being asked more and more to intervene in the life of the private individual, the relationship between the state and the individual. We should guard very carefully against arbitrary measures and encroachments on our human rights and fundamental freedom. In that respect, I think it is very desirable that we should reduce these rights and freedoms to writing so that we may have continually before us our objectives in that regard. It gives me a great deal of pleasure to be able to be here and support this measure for a Canadian bill of rights.

speakeroldname: Hon. E. D. Fulton (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext:
A very great deal has been said today in the course of this debate and also on Monday with regard to the bill of rights now before

the house, and it is obvious that between now and eleven o'clock I am not going to have sufficient time to make a complete review of what has been said.
I should like to start by attempting to outline for the house and particularly for the members of the opposition what they have obviously completely misconstrued and misinterpreted-the effect and extent of this bill and the concept that the government had in mind by way of a legislative enactment when it introduced this bill of rights. Our intention is to introduce a statute which will define the rights of all Canadians in clear and understandable language, a statute which will clearly authorize and assist the courts to interpret and protect those rights and which will, in addition, set a limit to executive and, in so far as it is possible or desirable, parliamentary authority to interfere with or abridge those rights. This, I submit, we have done. Ours is a draft bill of rights that he who runs may read.
I may have something to say later about this question of the language in which a bill of rights should be drafted, concerning which we heard so much from members of the opposition today and on Monday. At the present time I think it would suffice to say that had we used language as suggested, in particular by the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin), then certainly no one could understand it, let alone be inspired by the bill of rights which would have resulted.
What we wanted to do, and what I submit we have done, is draft a declaration of the rights applicable to all Canadians which will serve as indication to Canadians whether natural born or naturalized, of whatever origin, of whatever creed or whatever colour, that these rights are theirs by inheritance as Canadians. It has certainly been our intention to produce a bill in a compass which would enable it to be framed, if you will, and hung on the walls of our schools or churches or institutions of every sort so that a person might stand before it and read it and say: this is my inheritance as a Canadian.
Therefore we have, of course, been concerned not to be too long and verbose or too circumspect. We have been concerned to try to produce a declaration of what those rights are, couched in the simplest, the most effective terms, and we have been concerned to try to produce in addition an enforcement section, a section which makes it clear that those rights will be protected by the courts. This, again, is framed in language sufficiently clear that a person concerned about his rights will know what he is entitled to and how he will be able to go about asserting and protecting his rights.
Human Rights
There is at this stage just one point I want to make, and that is with reference to the suggestion by the Leader of the Opposition that perhaps the War Measures Act should be amended so as to make it clear that the governor in council would not have the right to deprive Canadian citizens of their citizenship by order in council even in wartime. It is obvious that this bill of rights and the debate in connection therewith will be of interest to Canadians of all sorts, including those who are naturalized Canadians as well as those who were born in this country, and therefore I think it is probably to be expected that the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) will make what appeal he can to the ethnic groups in Canada by making the sort of remark he made.
But I point out that the remarks he made had nothing to do with the bill of rights. He was talking about amendments to the War Measures Act. Why he should drag that in was perfectly obvious, but I will go no further than I have gone because one must not, of course, impute motives. However, I do want to emphasize that the Leader of the Opposition dragged in a reference to an amendment to the War Measures Act that has nothing to do with the bill of rights at all.
I want to point out, too, that he continually overlooked the fact that it was his government, when it introduced the citizenship act, that provided not one way but six ways by which Canadians could be deprived of their citizenship by order in council. The Leader of the Opposition omitted to mention that this government rectified this situation in 1958 by amending the citizenship act so that naturalized Canadians could not lose their citizenship by action of the governor in council except in two circumstances instead of six.
Perhaps I should outline the ways in which the previous act had taken power by order in council to deprive naturalized Canadians of their citizenship. Prior to September 6, 1958, when we amended the act, the citizenship act contained in subsection 1 of section 19 six broad causes which provided for the revocation of Canadian citizenship of persons other than natural-born Canadian citizens. There is no time for me to deal with them in detail tonight, but anyone who wishes may read them, and I have provided the reference. Because it was felt that these provisions discriminated unfairly against persons naturalized in Canada, we introduced a bill to amend the citizenship act providing that five of these six provisions be deleted. Of the original six, our bill retained only that one which provided for the revocation of Canadian citizenship in the case of persons who have obtained certificates of naturalization or citizenship by
